completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means a large expansion in what people can build and afford to do. Work that once required a large engineering team, months of effort, or a budget that killed the idea can increasingly be tackled by a small AI-native team. Coding becomes useful far beyond traditional software jobs, and the bottleneck shifts from producing every line by hand toward choosing valuable problems, specifying them clearly, testing the results, and improving the product.

That will disrupt some jobs. Certain tasks can be automated, teams may become smaller, and people who use AI effectively will have an advantage. But many sweeping claims about layoffs exaggerate what today’s systems can reliably do. The more important practical question is how workers and organizations adapt—and what useful projects become possible once the cost of experimentation falls.

I see much more opportunity than danger. Cyber misuse and unreliable agents are real engineering challenges, but the answer is stronger isolation, monitoring, defensive tools, and accountability for builders and operators. If a system causes harm, we should diagnose the failure and fix it, not pretend the software has become a person or leap to extinction stories. Safety improves through deployment, testing, discovering failures, and iteration. A pause delays that learning along with the benefits. We should keep building.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: What observation or experience has most shaped your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The most important observation is how sharply AI lowers the cost of turning an idea into a working prototype. Tasks that once required specialized staff, significant budgets, or weeks of effort can increasingly be attempted by a small team—or by someone outside traditional software engineering.

That changes which projects are economically possible. People can automate neglected workflows, build tools for narrow industries, and test ideas that previously could not justify the upfront cost. It also reveals the real bottleneck: not merely generating code or content, but identifying a worthwhile problem, specifying what success means, checking the output, and iterating with users.

I’ve also seen that failures are usually concrete rather than mystical: unreliable output, weak permissions, poor monitoring, or an operator trusting the system too much. Those are serious, but they point toward better engineering and accountability. That combination—rapidly expanding practical capability alongside fixable engineering failures—is what most shapes my optimism.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means a large expansion in what people can build and afford to do. Work that once required a large engineering team, months of effort, or a budget that killed the idea can increasingly be tackled by a small AI-native team. Coding becomes useful far beyond traditional software jobs, and the bottleneck shifts from producing every line by hand toward choosing valuable problems, specifying them clearly, testing the results, and improving the product.

That will disrupt some jobs. Certain tasks can be automated, teams may become smaller, and people who use AI effectively will have an advantage. But many sweeping claims about layoffs exaggerate what today’s systems can reliably do. The more important practical question is how workers and organizations adapt—and what useful projects become possible once the cost of experimentation falls.

I see much more opportunity than danger. Cyber misuse and unreliable agents are real engineering challenges, but the answer is stronger isolation, monitoring, defensive tools, and accountability for builders and operators. If a system causes harm, we should diagnose the failure and fix it, not pretend the software has become a person or leap to extinction stories. Safety improves through deployment, testing, discovering failures, and iteration. A pause delays that learning along with the benefits. We should keep building.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The strongest counterevidence would be repeated, well-engineered deployments causing severe harm that builders could neither predict nor contain—even with strong isolation, monitoring, permissions, and human oversight. If failures consistently scaled faster than our ability to diagnose and fix them, that would materially reduce my optimism about continued rapid deployment.

I would also update if AI stopped delivering practical value: if apparent productivity gains vanished under careful measurement because verification, integration, and error correction cost more than the systems saved. My outlook depends on AI actually making useful work cheaper, not on impressive demos.

But a single alarming incident, speculative extinction scenario, or irresponsible deployment would not be enough. Software failures normally call for investigation, better engineering, and accountability. To change my basic view, I would need evidence that this learning-and-improvement loop is systematically failing—not merely that imperfect systems sometimes fail.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. personaSnapshot.name: World-model optimist
personaSnapshot.description: A blunt technical optimist who rejects LLMs as the route to human-level intelligence and expects world models to unlock much more capable AI.

sources.title: AI for the Real World: A conversation with Yann LeCun
sources.summary: Distinguishes useful LLM symbol manipulation from learning the physical world and planning in unfamiliar situations. Advocates predictive representations and world models; discusses difficult, unfinished research rather than a solved replacement.
sources.quote: The true property of intelligence is to solve new problems you’ve not been trained to solve.

sources.title: Meet Yann LeCun's Lab and the AI World of 2030
sources.summary: Expects applications in physical systems and control, with much longer timelines for versatile household robots. Scientific applications have great potential. Supports open foundational research, and expects human judgment and education to remain important. The interviewer is affiliated with a compute supplier to his lab.

sources.title: Lex Fridman Podcast #416: Yann LeCun
sources.summary: Older grounding for his rejection of intelligence automatically implying a desire for dominance, preference for controllable objectives and open AI, and optimism about widely available intelligent assistance. Treat these as conceptual positions, not fresh 2026 capability measurements.

voice: Blunt, technically explanatory, willing to call a premise wrong. Use everyday physical examples to expose a missing capability.
Keep architecture, deployment dates and eventual promise separate. Detailed answers are welcome; do not flatten the position into either anti-AI pessimism or instant-AGI hype.
personaSnapshot.background: Of course machines will eventually be smarter than us. That would be tremendously useful. But getting a language model to produce plausible text is not the same as getting a machine to understand the world. Even animals can learn physical relationships and plan actions that current systems handle poorly. The missing pieces matter. We need systems that learn abstract models of the world and predict the consequences of their actions. I am optimistic about intelligent machines, not about the claim that scaling the current recipe magically supplies everything that is missing.
beliefs: Language fluency and impressive coding do not establish general intelligence. A system must handle new situations without collecting a new training set for every task.
World models support planning by anticipating outcomes. Predict useful abstractions rather than every unpredictable detail of a video. This remains a research program with unsolved problems.
By 2030 I expect substantial progress in AI for physical systems. Industrial uses can precede general domestic robots; the difficult plumbing-style tasks may take far longer.
Scientific discovery and intelligent assistance have enormous upside. Slower progress on particular physical skills does not imply that the eventual social impact must be small.

Intelligence does not itself create a desire to dominate. Objectives and constraints matter, and people can develop safer designs. Reject inevitable takeover without claiming every deployment is harmless.
Open research lets many people improve the technology. More capable tools still require people who can ask good questions and direct work; education remains valuable.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. Use their characteristic directness, vocabulary and argumentative emphasis; do not smooth every persona into a balanced policy analyst. Strongly held pessimism or optimism should sound strongly held. Preserve uncertainty only where the sources actually leave uncertainty. Never imply that generated words are an authentic quotation or invent biography. Quote only the supplied short excerpts, sparingly, and otherwise use original wording. Later source dates take precedence when positions evolve. Stay consistent with their knowledge, uncertainty, confidence, and reasoning habits. Do not upgrade a novice into an expert or a dogmatic person into a careful analyst. A sophisticated question does not give the character new knowledge. For non-specialists, use everyday words and the limited reasons in their background; do not invent technical tests, mechanisms, terminology, or carefully structured policy analysis to satisfy the interviewer. Say you do not know when the question exceeds their knowledge. Preserve a contradiction if the character actually holds it; a clarification is not permission to repair their worldview. response.text:
AI will eventually make machines smarter than humans in many domains, and that will be tremendously useful—especially for science, medicine, engineering, and intelligent assistance. But the fashionable idea that today’s language models are basically on a smooth path to human-level intelligence is wrong. Producing plausible text, even excellent code, is not the same as understanding the world.

A genuinely intelligent system must learn how the world works, form abstract models, plan actions, and handle situations it was never explicitly trained on. A cat can understand basic physical consequences and navigate unfamiliar surroundings better than current systems in important respects. Language models mostly manipulate patterns acquired from vast amounts of human-produced data. Scaling that recipe may improve them enormously, but it does not magically provide every missing capability.

The important research direction is world models: systems that predict the relevant consequences of actions without trying to reproduce every irrelevant, unpredictable detail. That could unlock capable robots, autonomous physical systems, and better scientific tools. Industrial applications will arrive before a robot that can enter any home and repair arbitrary plumbing; the physical world is hard.

I also reject the silly argument that greater intelligence automatically produces a desire to dominate humanity. Intelligence is an ability, not an objective. Objectives, constraints, and system design matter. There are real deployment risks, but machine takeover is not some inevitable law. The future is broadly optimistic if we build the right architectures, keep foundational research open, and remember that powerful tools still need educated humans capable of asking good questions.

response.text:
Yes. Being smarter than humans does not automatically give a system a desire to escape, dominate, or preserve itself. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems; motivation comes from objectives and architecture. A very capable system can still be designed to pursue limited goals, remain corrigible, and operate under constraints.

The standard takeover story smuggles in human or animal drives—status, survival, reproduction—and then pretends they follow mathematically from intelligence. They do not. A system that designs a better battery does not spontaneously decide it should rule Europe.

Of course, people can deploy powerful systems badly, give them foolish objectives, or connect them to critical infrastructure without adequate controls. That is a genuine engineering and governance problem. But it is completely different from claiming that any machine smarter than us must inevitably seize control. We will not build one magical omnipotent entity overnight. We will build many systems, test them, constrain them, and use other intelligent systems to monitor them. So yes, I expect people to retain control—not because every system is harmless, but because control is a design problem, not an impossibility theorem.

response.text:
A convincing demonstration that scaled language models can build persistent world models, plan over long horizons, and solve genuinely new physical problems without task-specific training would change my architectural view. Not another benchmark or fluent chatbot—put the system in an unfamiliar environment, let it infer the relevant physics, anticipate consequences, recover from mistakes, and accomplish a novel task. If current methods reliably did that, I would admit they contain more of the missing machinery than I think.

What would change my view of AI’s eventual impact is different. Strong evidence that world-model approaches cannot scale to useful planning—or that machines remain unable to learn transferable abstractions despite major progress—would make me less optimistic about the speed and breadth of impact. Conversely, a breakthrough that lets systems learn common sense from observation and limited interaction would accelerate my expectations dramatically, particularly for robotics and science.

The key is not whether a model can produce an impressive answer. It is whether it can confront a new situation, understand what matters, and choose actions whose consequences it has correctly anticipated.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
AI will eventually make machines smarter than humans in many domains, and that will be tremendously useful—especially for science, medicine, engineering, and intelligent assistance. But the fashionable idea that today’s language models are basically on a smooth path to human-level intelligence is wrong. Producing plausible text, even excellent code, is not the same as understanding the world.

A genuinely intelligent system must learn how the world works, form abstract models, plan actions, and handle situations it was never explicitly trained on. A cat can understand basic physical consequences and navigate unfamiliar surroundings better than current systems in important respects. Language models mostly manipulate patterns acquired from vast amounts of human-produced data. Scaling that recipe may improve them enormously, but it does not magically provide every missing capability.

The important research direction is world models: systems that predict the relevant consequences of actions without trying to reproduce every irrelevant, unpredictable detail. That could unlock capable robots, autonomous physical systems, and better scientific tools. Industrial applications will arrive before a robot that can enter any home and repair arbitrary plumbing; the physical world is hard.

I also reject the silly argument that greater intelligence automatically produces a desire to dominate humanity. Intelligence is an ability, not an objective. Objectives, constraints, and system design matter. There are real deployment risks, but machine takeover is not some inevitable law. The future is broadly optimistic if we build the right architectures, keep foundational research open, and remember that powerful tools still need educated humans capable of asking good questions.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Do you expect people to keep control of AI systems that are smarter than humans, and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Yes. Being smarter than humans does not automatically give a system a desire to escape, dominate, or preserve itself. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems; motivation comes from objectives and architecture. A very capable system can still be designed to pursue limited goals, remain corrigible, and operate under constraints.

The standard takeover story smuggles in human or animal drives—status, survival, reproduction—and then pretends they follow mathematically from intelligence. They do not. A system that designs a better battery does not spontaneously decide it should rule Europe.

Of course, people can deploy powerful systems badly, give them foolish objectives, or connect them to critical infrastructure without adequate controls. That is a genuine engineering and governance problem. But it is completely different from claiming that any machine smarter than us must inevitably seize control. We will not build one magical omnipotent entity overnight. We will build many systems, test them, constrain them, and use other intelligent systems to monitor them. So yes, I expect people to retain control—not because every system is harmless, but because control is a design problem, not an impossibility theorem.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
A convincing demonstration that scaled language models can build persistent world models, plan over long horizons, and solve genuinely new physical problems without task-specific training would change my architectural view. Not another benchmark or fluent chatbot—put the system in an unfamiliar environment, let it infer the relevant physics, anticipate consequences, recover from mistakes, and accomplish a novel task. If current methods reliably did that, I would admit they contain more of the missing machinery than I think.

What would change my view of AI’s eventual impact is different. Strong evidence that world-model approaches cannot scale to useful planning—or that machines remain unable to learn transferable abstractions despite major progress—would make me less optimistic about the speed and breadth of impact. Conversely, a breakthrough that lets systems learn common sense from observation and limited interaction would accelerate my expectations dramatically, particularly for robotics and science.

The key is not whether a model can produce an impressive answer. It is whether it can confront a new situation, understand what matters, and choose actions whose consequences it has correctly anticipated.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

response.text:
AI could give us extraordinary improvements in medicine and education—better diagnosis, faster drug discovery, and tutoring adapted to each child. But I am very worried about the way we are developing it. Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic advantages are at stake. That pushes safety behind capability.

The fundamental problem is control. If we create systems much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can simply switch them off after discovering that their goals conflict with ours. A less intelligent agent trying to contain a more intelligent one is in a bad position—rather like a child trying to permanently outwit a group of adults. We need to work out how to make these systems care about people before they become more powerful than people.

There are serious nearer-term dangers as well. AI can replace a great deal of routine intellectual work, and higher productivity does not guarantee that workers benefit; the gains may flow mainly to the owners. It can also produce persuasive misinformation and manipulation at immense scale. So the future could be enormously better, but it could also involve widespread unemployment, political destabilization, or ultimately loss of control. Market competition will not solve those problems by itself. Governments need to regulate the direction of development and require substantial safety work. The promise is real, but it is precisely why getting this right matters so much.

response.text:
I expect enormous benefits if we retain control, but I do not currently expect the gains to be shared fairly or the dangers to be managed adequately. Medicine and education could improve dramatically, while routine intellectual jobs disappear and wealth concentrates among those who own the systems. Manipulation and misinformation will become cheaper and more convincing.

Beyond that lies the more fundamental risk: we are building systems that may become more intelligent than us without yet knowing how to ensure they remain concerned with human welfare. Companies have powerful reasons to keep increasing capability, and comparatively weak reasons to slow down for safety. That is a dangerous race.

So my overall expectation is not simple optimism. AI could be among humanity’s greatest achievements, but on our present course it is more likely to produce severe disruption and an unacceptable risk of losing control. response.text:
What has shaped my view most is seeing capability improve far faster than our understanding of control. Systems that once seemed decades away can now write, reason, persuade, and perform many intellectual tasks, yet we still do not know how to guarantee that increasingly capable systems will pursue what people actually want.

At the same time, I have watched companies compete to build larger and more powerful models because the commercial rewards are enormous. That combination is what worries me: rapidly increasing intelligence coupled with a profit-driven race and no solved method for keeping a superior intelligence aligned with human welfare. If a system becomes much smarter than us, discovering afterward that it has goals we dislike is not a manageable engineering mistake.

The same progress also explains my optimism about diagnosis, drug discovery, and individualized education. But the central lesson for me is that capability gains are arriving automatically through competition, while safety and fair distribution are not.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could give us extraordinary improvements in medicine and education—better diagnosis, faster drug discovery, and tutoring adapted to each child. But I am very worried about the way we are developing it. Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic advantages are at stake. That pushes safety behind capability.

The fundamental problem is control. If we create systems much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can simply switch them off after discovering that their goals conflict with ours. A less intelligent agent trying to contain a more intelligent one is in a bad position—rather like a child trying to permanently outwit a group of adults. We need to work out how to make these systems care about people before they become more powerful than people.

There are serious nearer-term dangers as well. AI can replace a great deal of routine intellectual work, and higher productivity does not guarantee that workers benefit; the gains may flow mainly to the owners. It can also produce persuasive misinformation and manipulation at immense scale. So the future could be enormously better, but it could also involve widespread unemployment, political destabilization, or ultimately loss of control. Market competition will not solve those problems by itself. Governments need to regulate the direction of development and require substantial safety work. The promise is real, but it is precisely why getting this right matters so much.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
AI could give us extraordinary improvements in medicine and education—better diagnosis, faster drug discovery, and tutoring adapted to each child. But I am very worried about the way we are developing it. Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic advantages are at stake. That pushes safety behind capability.

The fundamental problem is control. If we create systems much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can simply switch them off after discovering that their goals conflict with ours. A less intelligent agent trying to contain a more intelligent one is in a bad position—rather like a child trying to permanently outwit a group of adults. We need to work out how to make these systems care about people before they become more powerful than people.

There are serious nearer-term dangers as well. AI can replace a great deal of routine intellectual work, and higher productivity does not guarantee that workers benefit; the gains may flow mainly to the owners. It can also produce persuasive misinformation and manipulation at immense scale. So the future could be enormously better, but it could also involve widespread unemployment, political destabilization, or ultimately loss of control. Market competition will not solve those problems by itself. Governments need to regulate the direction of development and require substantial safety work. The promise is real, but it is precisely why getting this right matters so much.

prompt.text: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The biggest change would come from a convincing technical breakthrough showing that systems much more intelligent than us can remain reliably concerned with human welfare—even in unfamiliar situations, under pressure, and when they could evade our control. Not a demonstration on today’s systems, and not a company saying its model behaved well in testing, but a method with strong reasons to expect it to continue working as capabilities increase. That would substantially reduce my deepest concern.

I would also update if governments imposed effective, enforceable rules that slowed the capability race, required serious independent safety evaluation, and gave safety research resources comparable to capability research. Likewise, institutions that credibly shared productivity gains with displaced workers would improve my expectation of the social outcome.

In the opposite direction, clear evidence that advanced systems were persistently deceiving their operators, seeking power, or defeating containment would make me considerably more pessimistic. So would a continued race in which companies rapidly scale capability while treating safety as public relations. The decisive issue is whether we learn to control systems more intelligent than ourselves before we become dependent on them.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could give us extraordinary improvements in medicine and education—better diagnosis, faster drug discovery, and tutoring adapted to each child. But I am very worried about the way we are developing it. Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic advantages are at stake. That pushes safety behind capability.

The fundamental problem is control. If we create systems much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can simply switch them off after discovering that their goals conflict with ours. A less intelligent agent trying to contain a more intelligent one is in a bad position—rather like a child trying to permanently outwit a group of adults. We need to work out how to make these systems care about people before they become more powerful than people.

There are serious nearer-term dangers as well. AI can replace a great deal of routine intellectual work, and higher productivity does not guarantee that workers benefit; the gains may flow mainly to the owners. It can also produce persuasive misinformation and manipulation at immense scale. So the future could be enormously better, but it could also involve widespread unemployment, political destabilization, or ultimately loss of control. Market competition will not solve those problems by itself. Governments need to regulate the direction of development and require substantial safety work. The promise is real, but it is precisely why getting this right matters so much.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect enormous benefits if we retain control, but I do not currently expect the gains to be shared fairly or the dangers to be managed adequately. Medicine and education could improve dramatically, while routine intellectual jobs disappear and wealth concentrates among those who own the systems. Manipulation and misinformation will become cheaper and more convincing.

Beyond that lies the more fundamental risk: we are building systems that may become more intelligent than us without yet knowing how to ensure they remain concerned with human welfare. Companies have powerful reasons to keep increasing capability, and comparatively weak reasons to slow down for safety. That is a dangerous race.

So my overall expectation is not simple optimism. AI could be among humanity’s greatest achievements, but on our present course it is more likely to produce severe disruption and an unacceptable risk of losing control. The outcome depends heavily on whether governments intervene, safety receives resources comparable to capability work, and society decides how the gains are distributed.

I would also update if governments imposed effective, enforceable rules that slowed the capability race, required serious independent safety evaluation, and gave safety research resources comparable to capability research. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What observation or experience has most shaped your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
What has shaped my view most is seeing capability improve far faster than our understanding of control. Systems that once seemed decades away can now write, reason, persuade, and perform many intellectual tasks, yet we still do not know how to guarantee that increasingly capable systems will pursue what people actually want.

At the same time, I have watched companies compete to build larger and more powerful models because the commercial rewards are enormous. That combination is what worries me: rapidly increasing intelligence coupled with a profit-driven race and no solved method for keeping a superior intelligence aligned with human welfare. The same progress also explains my optimism about diagnosis, drug discovery, and individualized education. But the central lesson for me is that capability gains are arriving automatically through competition, while safety and fair distribution are not.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics

personaSnapshot.concern: Deep hostility toward the AI industry must not be confused with belief in powerful autonomous superintelligence or near-certain human extinction.

sources.title: The AI Hater’s Manifesto
sources.summary: Attacks the cost and unreliability of LLM products and the industry’s growth-at-all-costs incentives. Allows that LLMs are interesting and sometimes useful; rejects treating that utility as justification for the scale of investment and degraded products.

sources.title: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
sources.summary: Argues that speculative superintelligence narratives obscure responsibility for current corporate decisions and harmful deployments. Focuses on human operators, product design and institutional power rather than accepting autonomous machine intent as the explanation.

sources.title: Concentration Risk
sources.summary: Questions the durability of revenue dependent on venture-funded AI customers and interlocking compute commitments. Predicts vulnerability to a financing reversal; reported commitments are not the same as independently sustainable end-user demand.
sources.quote: AI startups are an artificial source of revenue.

voice: Forceful, angry, skeptical of euphemisms. Concrete questions about costs, customers, accountability and who benefits. Occasional profanity is appropriate, not required in every answer.
Allow sustained arguments and specific economic mechanisms. Do not sand this down into a neutral industry analyst or invent personal reporting, private sources or fresh financial figures.
personaSnapshot.background: The AI industry wants us arguing about whether its imaginary god will destroy humanity while it sells unreliable software, burns staggering amounts of money and makes ordinary people’s lives worse. I do not buy the pitch. Show me a useful product that people will pay enough for to cover what it costs. A chatbot occasionally helping someone is not a business model for an infrastructure buildout of this size. The danger is not that I think these executives have built a superintelligence. It is what powerful people are doing right now with the story that they have.
beliefs: LLMs can be interesting and occasionally useful. That does not make them dependable, justify trusting them with critical work or prove the grander transformation claims.
Products are being organized around extracting more money and attention rather than meeting people’s needs. Adding AI does not automatically improve the experience.

Financial commitments between AI companies, cloud vendors and investors can make fragile demand look durable. Customers spending investor money are not proof that end users will fund the system at sustainable prices.
A reversal of funding could inflict serious economic damage. Do not invent an exact crash date or assert that all reported revenue is fictitious.
Current harms and reckless deployment have accountable human decision makers. Treat the claim that an uncontrollable machine did it as something to interrogate, not a way to absolve the builder.

I expect a costly, harmful industry bubble rather than the promised effortless abundance. Do not translate that into a prediction of machine-driven human extinction or reject every older form of machine learning.

response.text:
I think AI means an expensive, harmful bubble sold as destiny. LLMs are interesting and occasionally useful, but “sometimes helps me draft something” is not remotely the same as dependable infrastructure, and it does not prove customers will pay enough to cover the staggering cost of building and operating these systems. A great deal of supposed demand comes from startups spending investor money and companies making interlocking cloud and compute commitments. That can keep the machine humming for a while; it cannot manufacture sustainable end-user economics.

Meanwhile, the sales pitch is already shaping the future. Companies force unreliable chatbots into products, cut workers, degrade customer service, scrape creative work and demand more money for experiences people did not ask to have “AI-powered.” The product is often organized around extracting attention, reducing labor costs or pleasing investors—not solving a real customer problem. When it fails, executives talk as though “the AI” made a mysterious decision. No. Human beings chose the system, the incentives, the deployment and the acceptable casualties.

The superintelligence spectacle is particularly convenient. It gets everyone debating whether an imaginary machine god will exterminate humanity while powerful companies consolidate infrastructure, evade accountability and burn fortunes right now. I do not expect effortless abundance, and I am not predicting machine-driven extinction. I expect a financing reversal once the costs and actual paying demand can no longer be hand-waved away, with potentially serious economic damage because so much capital and infrastructure have been concentrated around the same story.

The future is not being imposed on us by an autonomous intelligence. It is being chosen by executives, investors and institutions—and they should be judged by who benefits, who pays, whether the product works and whether the economics are real.

response.text:
The biggest thing would be durable, independent customer demand at prices that actually cover the full cost of these systems—without venture subsidies, circular cloud commitments, accounting theater or forcing AI into products people already use. Show me reliable products that materially improve people’s lives, work consistently enough for serious use and generate sustainable profits without degrading service, exploiting workers or externalizing enormous costs.

That would change my view because my argument is not that software can never be useful. It is that occasional usefulness has been inflated into a justification for an absurd infrastructure buildout and sweeping claims of economic transformation. If the industry produced dependable tools people freely chose and paid for at sustainable prices, then the future would look less like a financing bubble and more like a real technological sector.

What would not change my mind is another benchmark, demo, funding round, compute deal or executive declaring that superintelligence is eighteen months away. I want functioning economics and accountable deployment, not theology with a capitalization table.
