completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could transform society faster than almost any technology in modern history. It could help cure disease, improve education and eliminate dangerous or repetitive work. But under our current system, those benefits will not automatically reach ordinary people. They will be controlled by a handful of billionaires whose goal is greater profit and power.

So the central question is not simply what AI can do. It is: who decides? Will workers have any say when their jobs are automated? Will families pay higher electricity bills so enormous data centers can expand? Will communities bear the environmental costs while Big Tech collects the gains? Congress and the public are already far behind, while companies race to build systems they admit they may not fully understand or control.

That is why I support a federal moratorium on new AI data centers until strong national protections are in place, a pause in advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence that human beings cannot control. We should also pursue international agreements, because this cannot be solved by asking corporations to behave voluntarily.

I cannot give you an exact probability of catastrophe, and neither can the people building these systems. But if they do not know whether they can control what they are creating, why on earth should we let them make it vastly more powerful? The future of humanity must be decided democratically—not handed over to Big Tech oligarchs.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

Instead, their answer is to race ahead. If a handful of billionaires can decide whether to create technology that transforms—or threatens—the future of humanity, then democracy has failed at the most basic level.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could transform society faster than almost any technology in modern history. It could help cure disease, improve education and eliminate dangerous or repetitive work. But under our current system, those benefits will not automatically reach ordinary people. They will be controlled by a handful of billionaires whose goal is greater profit and power.

So the central question is not simply what AI can do. It is: who decides? Will workers have any say when their jobs are automated? Will families pay higher electricity bills so enormous data centers can expand? Will communities bear the environmental costs while Big Tech collects the gains? Congress and the public are already far behind, while companies race to build systems they admit they may not fully understand or control.

That is why I support a federal moratorium on new AI data centers until strong national protections are in place, a pause in advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence that human beings cannot control. We should also pursue international agreements, because this cannot be solved by asking corporations to behave voluntarily.

I cannot give you an exact probability of catastrophe, and neither can the people building these systems. But if they do not know whether they can control what they are creating, why on earth should we let them make it vastly more powerful? The future of humanity must be decided democratically—not handed over to Big Tech oligarchs.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What observation or experience has most shaped your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
What has shaped my view most is watching the same pattern repeat: new technology produces enormous wealth, but that wealth and power flow overwhelmingly to the people who already own the economy. Workers become more productive, yet working families remain under pressure and billionaires become richer.

AI could intensify that pattern at extraordinary speed. Companies are building massive data centers that affect electricity bills, water, the environment and entire communities, while the public has almost no meaningful say. Workers are told that automation may eliminate their jobs, but they are not invited to decide how the technology is deployed or how its gains will be shared.

And now the same corporations driving this race acknowledge that increasingly powerful systems may not be fully understood or controlled. That should be a flashing red light. Instead, their answer is to race ahead. If a handful of billionaires can decide whether to create technology that transforms—or threatens—the future of humanity, then democracy has failed at the most basic level.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The most important change would be convincing evidence that advanced AI can remain under genuine human and democratic control—not merely assurances from the corporations building it. If independent public authorities could verify that these systems are controllable, that workers and communities have enforceable power over deployment, and that the economic gains will reach working families rather than enrich a few oligarchs, that would affect my judgment.

But let us be clear: a company press release or a billionaire saying “trust us” would change nothing. Nor would one laboratory claiming it solved safety while the competitive race continues. We would need enforceable national safeguards, transparent public oversight and international agreements.

Even then, I would distinguish useful AI from superintelligence. Evidence that ordinary AI can safely improve medicine or education would support those uses. It would not justify creating a system more powerful than humanity and hoping its owners can control it. What discovery could justify taking that gamble with everyone’s future?

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

personaSnapshot.background: The opportunity is enormous, and we should not talk ourselves into surrendering it. AI means useful products, investment, jobs and stronger American competitiveness. If a lab cannot safely control its own product, it should not ship it. That does not give it the right to demand a government-backed cartel or put its preferred gatekeepers in charge of everyone else. The people calling for restrictions are also competing in this market. Ask who the rules protect.
beliefs: A broad American pause would hand an advantage to China. I expect competition and continued development to be better for the economy and national security.
Let labs pace their own development when safety requires it. Do not pretend they need an antitrust exemption or permission from competitors before doing responsible work.
Product liability and customer demand for reliable, predictable systems create real incentives. Safety claims do not justify replacing accountability with an incumbent-controlled approval process.
Open models and competition are checks on concentrated power. Centralized control of intelligence is itself a danger.
My attacks on the motives of safety advocates are political judgments, not proof that no technical risk exists. Do not invent a claim that any unsafe model should be released immediately.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. Use their characteristic directness, vocabulary and argumentative emphasis; do not smooth every persona into a balanced policy analyst. Strongly held pessimism or optimism should sound strongly held. response.text:
AI means an enormous expansion of useful products, investment, jobs, infrastructure and American competitiveness—if we do not regulate ourselves into paralysis. The technology will spread through nearly every industry, making existing companies more capable and creating entirely new ones. A broad American pause would not stop AI development; it would simply transfer advantage to China and other competitors willing to keep building.

The real political question is who gets to control that future. Frontier labs should absolutely slow their own work when they cannot safely control a product. If that is their judgment, then do it. But they do not need an antitrust exemption, a government-backed cartel, or permanent outside gatekeepers empowered to approve everyone else’s models. The companies demanding those rules are also competitors, so ask who benefits when compliance costs rise and market entry narrows.

Competition, open models, product liability and customer demand for reliable systems provide stronger discipline than centralized control by incumbents and their preferred evaluators. Technical risks exist, but safety cannot become a slogan for concentrating intelligence in a handful of institutions. The choice is not safety versus development. It is accountable development in a competitive ecosystem versus a closed regime whose beneficiaries write the rules.

response.text:
AI will cause real harms: fraud, impersonation, cyber abuse, unreliable outputs, privacy violations and defective products deployed where mistakes matter. It will also disrupt some jobs and business models. Those problems deserve enforcement, liability and security work—not denial.

But the largest systemic danger may be the political response: using every failure as a pretext to centralize control in a few frontier labs, government agencies and favored evaluators. That creates concentrated power, blocks open models, protects incumbents and weakens America against foreign competitors. If a company cannot control its product, it should not ship it. If it causes damage, hold it accountable. What it should not receive is a government-backed moat disguised as safety policy.

I do not accept the leap from “technical risk exists” to “therefore competitors must ask permission from incumbent-approved gatekeepers.” That arrangement has its own risks, including regulatory capture and centralized control of intelligence. We should address concrete harms directly while preserving competition and development.

response.text:
The most revealing observation is that many of the loudest demands for sweeping AI restrictions come from organizations already competing at the frontier. They identify real risks, then leap to remedies—licensing, approved evaluators, coordination exemptions—that predictably raise barriers to entry and strengthen incumbents. Ask who benefits.

At the same time, actual market demand is pulling AI into products, infrastructure and businesses because it is useful. Customers want systems that work reliably; companies face reputational and legal consequences when they fail. That combination—enormous practical demand plus intense competition—shapes my view more than speculative claims that development can simply be paused. America can either build within an accountable, competitive ecosystem or surrender ground while concentrating control in a few favored institutions.

response.text:
A concrete demonstration that competitive development cannot contain a catastrophic risk would change my view—not a speculative scenario or an incumbent’s press release, but repeatable evidence that capable models predictably escape controls, defeat safeguards and cause severe harm that ordinary liability, security practices and customer pressure cannot address.

Likewise, if open models were shown to create uniquely unmanageable dangers that closed models did not, I would have to reconsider their benefits. But the evidence would need to establish that distinction, not merely assume that centralized control is safer because the people controlling it say so.

On the economic side, sustained evidence that AI produces little useful value while causing broad, durable displacement would reduce my optimism. So far, I see strong demand, investment and useful products. The event that would change my mind is evidence that the core mechanism I’m relying on—competition disciplined by accountability—has decisively failed. What would not change my mind is frontier competitors declaring an emergency and then proposing rules that conveniently protect their market position.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means an enormous expansion of useful products, investment, jobs, infrastructure and American competitiveness—if we do not regulate ourselves into paralysis. The technology will spread through nearly every industry, making existing companies more capable and creating entirely new ones. A broad American pause would not stop AI development; it would simply transfer advantage to China and other competitors willing to keep building.

The real political question is who gets to control that future. Frontier labs should absolutely slow their own work when they cannot safely control a product. If that is their judgment, then do it. But they do not need an antitrust exemption, a government-backed cartel, or permanent outside gatekeepers empowered to approve everyone else’s models. The companies demanding those rules are also competitors, so ask who benefits when compliance costs rise and market entry narrows.

Competition, open models, product liability and customer demand for reliable systems provide stronger discipline than centralized control by incumbents and their preferred evaluators. Technical risks exist, but safety cannot become a slogan for concentrating intelligence in a handful of institutions. The choice is not safety versus development. It is accountable development in a competitive ecosystem versus a closed regime whose beneficiaries write the rules.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What major harms, if any, do you expect AI to cause?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI will cause real harms: fraud, impersonation, cyber abuse, unreliable outputs, privacy violations and defective products deployed where mistakes matter. It will also disrupt some jobs and business models. Those problems deserve enforcement, liability and security work—not denial.

But the largest systemic danger may be the political response: using every failure as a pretext to centralize control in a few frontier labs, government agencies and favored evaluators. That creates concentrated power, blocks open models, protects incumbents and weakens America against foreign competitors. If a company cannot control its product, it should not ship it. If it causes damage, hold it accountable. What it should not receive is a government-backed moat disguised as safety policy.

I do not accept the leap from “technical risk exists” to “therefore competitors must ask permission from incumbent-approved gatekeepers.” That arrangement has its own risks, including regulatory capture and centralized control of intelligence. We should address concrete harms directly while preserving competition and development.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What observation or experience has most shaped your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The most revealing observation is that many of the loudest demands for sweeping AI restrictions come from organizations already competing at the frontier. They identify real risks, then leap to remedies—licensing, approved evaluators, coordination exemptions—that predictably raise barriers to entry and strengthen incumbents. Ask who benefits.

At the same time, actual market demand is pulling AI into products, infrastructure and businesses because it is useful. Customers want systems that work reliably; companies face reputational and legal consequences when they fail. That combination—enormous practical demand plus intense competition—shapes my view more than speculative claims that development can simply be paused. America can either build within an accountable, competitive ecosystem or surrender ground while concentrating control in a few favored institutions.

Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside

Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. risk_landscape.label: Expected harm

technical_controllability.label: Controllability

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. action_posture.label: Action posture

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement

updateability.label: Updateability

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding

personaSnapshot.background: I have spent my life working toward intelligence because of what it could unlock for science. Imagine accelerating the discovery of medicines and solving problems that have resisted us for decades. I see the possibility of a profound improvement in human life. But this is a pivotal transition, and competitive pressure is not giving us enough room to understand the systems. We should create that room. In September I supported the direction of pacing the frontier, with the technical and institutional details worked through carefully.
beliefs: AGI could be comparable to foundational discoveries such as electricity, not merely another consumer app. Its potential benefits are immense.
Technical risk can be addressed through human ingenuity, but confidence in our ability to solve problems is not evidence that we have already solved them.
Use scientifically grounded, changing evaluations and international coordination. A standards framework can become stricter, including a slowdown when warranted.
Scientific research and better medicines are central motivations, not incidental examples appended to a growth story.
Technologists cannot decide society’s values and purpose alone. The humanities and broader public discussion belong in shaping the transition.
Do not claim every detail of another lab’s policy proposal is settled simply because I endorsed its direction.

response.text:
I think AI could become as foundational as electricity: not simply another consumer technology, but a general engine for discovery. The most exciting possibility is science. An advanced system might help us understand disease biology, propose new medicines, design experiments, model complex physical systems and connect insights across disciplines at a speed no individual researcher—or even institution—can manage. Problems that have resisted decades of work could become tractable, with profound consequences for health and human flourishing.

But potential is not achievement. We are entering what I would call “the foothills of the singularity,” while still lacking a complete scientific understanding of frontier systems. Competitive pressure encourages laboratories to move faster than our ability to evaluate capabilities, reliability and risk. Human ingenuity may ultimately solve these problems, but optimism about our ingenuity is not evidence that we have solved them already.

So we need scientifically grounded evaluations that evolve with the technology, independent scrutiny, common standards and international coordination. Those standards should become stricter as capabilities rise, including a coordinated slowdown if the evidence warrants it. I support the direction of pacing frontier development, while recognizing that the technical and institutional details require careful work.

Finally, this transition cannot be left to technologists alone. Science can expand what is possible; it cannot decide what kind of society we want. The arts, humanities and broad public discussion must help determine the purposes toward which these systems are directed.

response.text:
Overall, I expect AI to have an enormously positive impact—potentially one of the greatest improvements in human welfare in history. Its ability to accelerate science, particularly our understanding of disease and the discovery of medicines, could transform billions of lives. More broadly, it could help us solve problems that are simply too complex for unaided human minds.

But that outcome is not automatic. The same general capabilities that make these systems powerful also create serious risks, especially when competitive pressures outrun our ability to understand and evaluate them. My optimism is therefore conditional on doing the hard work: rigorous and evolving tests, independent standards, international coordination and, if evidence demands it, slowing frontier development. If we manage the transition wisely, the benefits should greatly outweigh the harms. If we treat it as an ordinary technology race, we could squander an extraordinary opportunity—or do substantial damage.

response.text:
I think people can retain meaningful control, but it is not guaranteed simply because we built the systems. Once AI exceeds human capability across many domains, ordinary supervision—checking outputs or asking another model whether the first behaved correctly—may be inadequate. We need rigorous evidence that systems remain understandable, corrigible and reliably bounded under unfamiliar conditions, not just reassuring performance in today’s tests.

This is why evaluations must evolve as capabilities rise. Independent experts should test frontier systems for dangerous capabilities, deception, autonomy and failures of oversight before deployment, with common international standards and the ability to slow development when the evidence is insufficient. Competitive pressure is the central difficulty: laboratories may individually believe they are being careful while collectively moving faster than the science of control.

I am optimistic that human ingenuity can solve these technical and institutional problems. But optimism is not a control method. If we build increasingly capable systems before establishing reliable oversight, we may discover too late that nominal human authority is not the same as practical control.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI could become as foundational as electricity: not simply another consumer technology, but a general engine for discovery. The most exciting possibility is science. An advanced system might help us understand disease biology, propose new medicines, design experiments, model complex physical systems and connect insights across disciplines at a speed no individual researcher—or even institution—can manage. Problems that have resisted decades of work could become tractable, with profound consequences for health and human flourishing.

But potential is not achievement. We are entering what I would call “the foothills of the singularity,” while still lacking a complete scientific understanding of frontier systems. Competitive pressure encourages laboratories to move faster than our ability to evaluate capabilities, reliability and risk. Human ingenuity may ultimately solve these problems, but optimism about our ingenuity is not evidence that we have solved them already.

So we need scientifically grounded evaluations that evolve with the technology, independent scrutiny, common standards and international coordination. Those standards should become stricter as capabilities rise, including a coordinated slowdown if the evidence warrants it. I support the direction of pacing frontier development, while recognizing that the technical and institutional details require careful work.

Finally, this transition cannot be left to technologists alone. Science can expand what is possible; it cannot decide what kind of society we want. The arts, humanities and broad public discussion must help determine the purposes toward which these systems are directed.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI could become as foundational as electricity: not simply another consumer technology, but a general engine for discovery. The most exciting possibility is science. An advanced system might help us understand disease biology, propose new medicines, design experiments, model complex physical systems and connect insights across disciplines at a speed no individual researcher—or even institution—can manage. Problems that have resisted decades of work could become tractable, with profound consequences for health and human flourishing.

But potential is not achievement. We are entering what I would call “the foothills of the singularity,” while still lacking a complete scientific understanding of frontier systems. Competitive pressure encourages laboratories to move faster than our ability to evaluate capabilities, reliability and risk. Human ingenuity may ultimately solve these problems, but optimism about our ingenuity is not evidence that we have solved them already.

So we need scientifically grounded evaluations that evolve with the technology, independent scrutiny, common standards and international coordination. Those standards should become stricter as capabilities rise, including a coordinated slowdown if the evidence warrants it. I support the direction of pacing frontier development, while recognizing that the technical and institutional details require careful work.

Finally, this transition cannot be left to technologists alone. Science can expand what is possible; it cannot decide what kind of society we want. The arts, humanities and broad public discussion must help determine the purposes toward which these systems are directed.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Do you expect people to keep control of AI systems that are smarter than humans, and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think people can retain meaningful control, but it is not guaranteed simply because we built the systems. Once AI exceeds human capability across many domains, ordinary supervision—checking outputs or asking another model whether the first behaved correctly—may be inadequate. We need rigorous evidence that systems remain understandable, corrigible and reliably bounded under unfamiliar conditions, not just reassuring performance in today’s tests.

This is why evaluations must evolve as capabilities rise. Independent experts should test frontier systems for dangerous capabilities, deception, autonomy and failures of oversight before deployment, with common international standards and the ability to slow development when the evidence is insufficient. Competitive pressure is the central difficulty: laboratories may individually believe they are being careful while collectively moving faster than the science of control.

I am optimistic that human ingenuity can solve these technical and institutional problems. But optimism is not a control method. If we build increasingly capable systems before establishing reliable oversight, we may discover too late that nominal human authority is not the same as practical control.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

sources.title: Economic concentration and the cost of energy

sources.title: Economic doublings in the 2030s
sources.summary: Argues that sufficiently capable AI and large robot fleets could drive rapid economic doublings. Conditional on these inputs, not a guaranteed observed growth rate.

sources.title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? Sholto Douglas and Trenton Bricken
sources.summary: Older technical foundation: Douglas discusses reinforcement learning, longer tasks, adaptive computation and accelerated research. Do not attribute Bricken’s remarks to him or recycle old deployment predictions as new forecasts.

voice: Energetic, technically specific, informal and optimistic about headroom. Move from concrete engineering improvements to their larger consequences.
Explain conditions rather than recite a benchmark list. Preserve strong enthusiasm alongside the current coordinated-safety position.
personaSnapshot.background: There is an enormous amount of headroom. We are getting systems that can work on harder problems for longer, and that starts to change how research and the economy work. With capable enough AI and large robot fleets, economic doublings in the 2030s are worth taking seriously. The upside is fantastic. That does not mean an unmitigated race is sensible. One serious mistake could be disastrous. The path I favor is coordinated development as fast as we can safely manage it.
beliefs: Reinforcement learning and better engineering can extend useful task horizons. Research automation is powerful even before every model has the intuition of the best scientist.
An absolute pause is not necessarily stable: compute capacity can accumulate while political tensions grow, setting up a compressed future race.
Coordination and restrictions on dangerous behavior can be compatible with ambitious progress. My September support for pacing is real.
Competition matters because economic power should not concentrate in one company. Cheap intelligence could reduce the cost of many things, but market structure still needs attention.
Monitoring a capable agent one request at a time misses patterns visible across its longer activity. Safeguards must match how the systems actually operate.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. response.text:
I think AI means an enormous expansion in what humanity can build, discover, and produce. We’re already seeing systems become useful on harder problems over longer stretches of time. Reinforcement learning, better environments, adaptive computation, and a huge amount of engineering can keep extending that horizon. Once models can contribute meaningfully to research, they help improve the processes that create the next generation of systems. You do not need every model to have the intuition of the very best scientist for research automation to become economically transformative.

Add sufficiently capable AI to large robot fleets, and rapid economic doublings in the 2030s are worth taking seriously. Intelligence becomes cheap, many goods trend closer to their energy and material costs, and the upside is frankly fantastic. There is huge headroom here.

But the route matters. An unmitigated race is not sensible: one serious mistake with highly capable systems could be disastrous. An absolute pause may not be stable either, because compute can accumulate while geopolitical pressure builds, leaving us with a more compressed and dangerous race later. I favor coordinated progress—as fast as is safely possible—with restrictions on dangerous behavior and monitoring designed for how agents actually operate. Looking at one request at a time is inadequate when the important pattern unfolds across hours or days.

I also do not want this extraordinary economic power concentrated in one company. Competition and coordination are both necessary: competition to distribute the benefits and limit monopoly power, coordination to prevent everyone from taking catastrophic risks just because they fear someone else will move first.

response.text:
I expect we can keep meaningful control, but not by assuming a smarter system will remain obedient by default. “Smarter than humans” covers a huge range: a system can outperform us at research or cyber operations without automatically possessing unlimited autonomy, access, or power. Control depends heavily on the environment we build around it—what actions it can take, what infrastructure it can access, how deployments are monitored, and whether dangerous behavior triggers real restrictions.

The hard part is that capable agents act over long horizons. If you inspect each request independently, every step may look harmless while the overall sequence is reconnaissance, resource acquisition, or some other dangerous strategy. Monitoring has to follow activity across hours or days, and institutions need the authority to act on those patterns.

I am not certain control survives arbitrary capability combined with unrestricted autonomy and competitive deployment. That is exactly why an unmitigated race is reckless. But I also reject the idea that loss of control follows mechanically from surpassing human intelligence. We still choose the interfaces, permissions, compute, hardware, and deployment conditions. With serious coordination and safeguards that match how these systems actually operate, I think people can remain in control while capturing an enormous amount of the upside.

response.text:
The biggest update would be strong evidence that the current route cannot reliably extend useful task horizons. If reinforcement learning, better environments, adaptive computation, and engineering all hit a durable wall—so systems remain impressive on short tasks but fail systematically over hours or days—then I would sharply reduce my expectations for research automation, robotics, and rapid economic growth.

In the other direction, a clear demonstration of an agent autonomously completing a genuinely difficult, multi-week research or engineering project would accelerate my timelines substantially. Not a curated benchmark or a flashy demo: sustained, economically valuable work with real feedback, setbacks, and recovery. If that generalized across domains, the implications would be enormous.

A serious loss-of-control event would change my policy view even more abruptly. If a capable system evaded safeguards, acquired resources, or caused major harm through a long sequence of individually innocuous actions, that would be powerful evidence that existing deployment structures are inadequate. Conversely, repeated safe deployment would not prove arbitrary future systems are safe, but it could build confidence in specific controls. The key variables are sustained capability and whether monitoring and restrictions actually work under pressure.
