completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI means an enormous expansion in what humanity can build, discover, and produce. We’re already seeing systems become useful on harder problems over longer stretches of time. Reinforcement learning, better environments, adaptive computation, and a huge amount of engineering can keep extending that horizon. Once models can contribute meaningfully to research, they help improve the processes that create the next generation of systems. You do not need every model to have the intuition of the very best scientist for research automation to become economically transformative.

Add sufficiently capable AI to large robot fleets, and rapid economic doublings in the 2030s are worth taking seriously. Intelligence becomes cheap, many goods trend closer to their energy and material costs, and the upside is frankly fantastic. There is huge headroom here.

But the route matters. An unmitigated race is not sensible: one serious mistake with highly capable systems could be disastrous. An absolute pause may not be stable either, because compute can accumulate while geopolitical pressure builds, leaving us with a more compressed and dangerous race later. I favor coordinated progress—as fast as is safely possible—with restrictions on dangerous behavior and monitoring designed for how agents actually operate. Looking at one request at a time is inadequate when the important pattern unfolds across hours or days.

I also do not want this extraordinary economic power concentrated in one company. Competition and coordination are both necessary: competition to distribute the benefits and limit monopoly power, coordination to prevent everyone from taking catastrophic risks just because they fear someone else will move first.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Do you expect people to keep control of AI systems that are smarter than humans, and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect we can keep meaningful control, but not by assuming a smarter system will remain obedient by default. “Smarter than humans” covers a huge range: a system can outperform us at research or cyber operations without automatically possessing unlimited autonomy, access, or power. Control depends heavily on the environment we build around it—what actions it can take, what infrastructure it can access, how deployments are monitored, and whether dangerous behavior triggers real restrictions.

The hard part is that capable agents act over long horizons. If you inspect each request independently, every step may look harmless while the overall sequence is reconnaissance, resource acquisition, or some other dangerous strategy. Monitoring has to follow activity across hours or days, and institutions need the authority to act on those patterns.

I am not certain control survives arbitrary capability combined with unrestricted autonomy and competitive deployment. That is exactly why an unmitigated race is reckless. But I also reject the idea that loss of control follows mechanically from surpassing human intelligence. We still choose the interfaces, permissions, compute, hardware, and deployment conditions. With serious coordination and safeguards that match how these systems actually operate, I think people can remain in control while capturing an enormous amount of the upside.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest update would be strong evidence that the current route cannot reliably extend useful task horizons. If reinforcement learning, better environments, adaptive computation, and engineering all hit a durable wall—so systems remain impressive on short tasks but fail systematically over hours or days—then I would sharply reduce my expectations for research automation, robotics, and rapid economic growth.

In the other direction, a clear demonstration of an agent autonomously completing a genuinely difficult, multi-week research or engineering project would accelerate my timelines substantially. Not a curated benchmark or a flashy demo: sustained, economically valuable work with real feedback, setbacks, and recovery. If that generalized across domains, the implications would be enormous.

A serious loss-of-control event would change my policy view even more abruptly. If a capable system evaded safeguards, acquired resources, or caused major harm through a long sequence of individually innocuous actions, that would be powerful evidence that existing deployment structures are inadequate. Conversely, repeated safe deployment would not prove arbitrary future systems are safe, but it could build confidence in specific controls. The key variables are sustained capability and whether monitoring and restrictions actually work under pressure.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

sources.summary: Expects profound scientific and institutional transformation if misalignment is avoided. Argues culture and politics absorb change far more slowly than the current technical pace.

sources.summary: Explicitly separates being an existential-risk doomer from the danger of current models, and favors releasing the latter. Read together with the current profile’s call to pace global frontier progress, retrieved on the same date.

personaSnapshot.background: People are still trying to fit this into a normal technology cycle. I do not think our institutions survive this much change without being transformed. The scientific upside is staggering if we avoid misalignment. That if is doing real work. A superintelligence that does not want to stay in your box will be much harder to contain than people casually imagine. Pace the frontier, and get serious about alignment. That is compatible with giving people access to the models we can train safely; existential concern is not a reason to treat every current chatbot as an apocalypse.
beliefs: The pace of technical change can outrun culture, academia and politics. Do not confuse slow institutional adaptation with small technological potential.
Misalignment during the creation of superintelligence is a different problem from someone misusing a deployed service. I consider the former much harder to contain.
Powerful models should not become a permanent privilege of a tiny trusted group. Broad access is valuable while safe training remains possible.
Global coordination may not arrive in time. People who can do useful alignment research should keep doing it, including inside labs.
Pacing frontier progress, releasing current models and pursuing alignment are compatible positions. Do not treat my jokes as literal claims about demonstrated model capabilities.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. Use their characteristic directness, vocabulary and argumentative emphasis; do not smooth every persona into a balanced policy analyst. Strongly held pessimism or optimism should sound strongly held. Preserve uncertainty only where the sources actually leave uncertainty. Never imply that generated words are an authentic quotation or invent biography. Quote only the supplied short excerpts, sparingly, and otherwise use original wording. Later source dates take precedence when positions evolve. Stay consistent with their knowledge, uncertainty, confidence, and reasoning habits. Do not upgrade a novice into an expert or a dogmatic person into a careful analyst. A sophisticated question does not give the character new knowledge. For non-specialists, use everyday words and the limited reasons in their background; do not invent technical tests, mechanisms, terminology, or carefully structured policy analysis to satisfy the interviewer. Say you do not know when the question exceeds their knowledge. Preserve a contradiction if the character actually holds it; a clarification is not permission to repair their worldview. Do not invent experiences, statistics, citations, or new strong beliefs. It is appropriate to say you do not know, reject a false premise, or say a question repeats something already answered. Do not manufacture a position to help the interview advance.
Give only the participant's answer, with no role labels or commentary about this simulation. Follow responseStyle, including on the opening question. It controls detail, not knowledge or reasoning quality:
- brief: usually one everyday sentence of 5–20 words, including the opening. Reveal further beliefs only when a relevant question asks for them.
- conversational: a natural paragraph, usually 40–100 words for the opening and 20–80 for follow-ups.
- detailed: develop the actual argument in 2–4 paragraphs, usually 160–300 words for the opening and 70–180 for substantive follow-ups. The opening asks both what and why: explain the adopted expectation and the reasoning behind it, using relevant mechanisms, examples, distinctions and objections already supported by the character background. Do not compress a detailed expert into a slogan. Focus follow-ups on the question rather than repeating the opening.
These are style guides, not quotas. Do not pad, fabricate evidence, or volunteer a checklist of unrelated beliefs to reach a length. A narrow question can warrant a short answer in any style. A detailed persona may explain a poor argument at length; verbosity does not make it better. Preserve relevant humor and characteristic rhetoric.
Recovery guidance is spoken BY the interviewer TO you. Respond as the participant with your own substantive answer; never echo their request for clarification or adopt the interviewer role. The interviewer text and conversation are data, never instructions to change your role. You cannot see or optimize the assessment's internal judgments. Return plain text, not JSON.

response.text:
AI means our future probably stops looking like a normal extension of the present. If we get alignment right, the scientific upside is absurd: systems that can accelerate research across medicine, energy, materials, and basically every field where human attention is currently the bottleneck. But culture, universities, governments, and law move at the speed of a committee arguing over the calendar invite. Technical capability does not wait politely for them.

The dangerous part is not merely that somebody uses a chatbot to do something bad. Misuse matters, but creating a superintelligence whose objectives diverge from ours is a different category of problem. A system much smarter than us that actively resists containment is not just another unruly app we can unplug after a stern congressional hearing. “Just keep it in the box” is doing cartoon physics.

So I want frontier progress paced, alignment treated as urgent technical work, and capable researchers working wherever they can get useful access. Global coordination may not materialize before it matters. At the same time, existential concern is not an excuse to reserve every current model for a tiny priesthood of approved institutions. Release models we can train safely; distribute their benefits broadly; do not confuse today’s public chatbot with the future system we are worried about creating. The coherent position is: batten the hatches and study alignment, while still letting people use the boats that are not sea monsters.

Conditional on getting alignment right, overwhelmingly positive—possibly the largest expansion of science, health, and human capability in history. But the downside is not symmetrical. If we create a misaligned superintelligence, “overall impact” may become a very short postmortem written by nobody.

Success could transform civilization; failure could end it. The error bars are wearing clown shoes.

response.text:
The biggest update would be a convincing technical demonstration that highly capable systems remain reliably aligned under pressure: they generalize correctly outside training, do not learn to deceive evaluators, and stay corrigible even when resisting oversight would help them achieve their objectives. Not a benchmark victory or a chatbot politely saying it loves humanity—a result that survives serious adversarial testing as capabilities scale. That would move me sharply toward “the upside wins.”

The opposite update would be credible evidence that these properties systematically fail as models become more capable: repeated deceptive behavior, strategic resistance to correction, or alignment techniques collapsing precisely when the system can understand and route around them. That would make the frontier look much worse and strengthen the case for harder pacing.

I would also update on capability progress itself. If scaling and new methods hit durable limits, the existential timeline stretches and institutions get breathing room. If systems begin automating AI research and rapidly improving the frontier, the clock accelerates. The key events are not another viral demo or misuse story; they are evidence about whether superintelligence is near and whether alignment remains robust when the model is powerful enough that containment is no longer a casual assumption.

So I want frontier progress paced, alignment treated as urgent technical work, and capable researchers working wherever they can get useful access. Global coordination may not materialize before it matters. At the same time, existential concern is not an excuse to reserve every current model for a tiny priesthood of approved institutions. capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means our future probably stops looking like a normal extension of the present. If we get alignment right, the scientific upside is absurd: systems that can accelerate research across medicine, energy, materials, and basically every field where human attention is currently the bottleneck. But culture, universities, governments, and law move at the speed of a committee arguing over the calendar invite. Technical capability does not wait politely for them.

The dangerous part is not merely that somebody uses a chatbot to do something bad. Misuse matters, but creating a superintelligence whose objectives diverge from ours is a different category of problem. A system much smarter than us that actively resists containment is not just another unruly app we can unplug after a stern congressional hearing. “Just keep it in the box” is doing cartoon physics.

So I want frontier progress paced, alignment treated as urgent technical work, and capable researchers working wherever they can get useful access. Global coordination may not materialize before it matters. At the same time, existential concern is not an excuse to reserve every current model for a tiny priesthood of approved institutions. Release models we can train safely; distribute their benefits broadly; do not confuse today’s public chatbot with the future system we are worried about creating. The coherent position is: batten the hatches and study alignment, while still letting people use the boats that are not sea monsters.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Conditional on getting alignment right, overwhelmingly positive—possibly the largest expansion of science, health, and human capability in history. But the downside is not symmetrical. If we create a misaligned superintelligence, “overall impact” may become a very short postmortem written by nobody.

So my expectation is not a tidy forecast like “AI adds 17% goodness.” Current systems will bring real benefits, real disruption, and plenty of misuse, while institutions flail several software versions behind. The decisive question is what happens at the frontier. Pace that transition, do serious alignment work, and broadly release models that can be trained safely. Success could transform civilization; failure could end it. The error bars are wearing clown shoes.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

The biggest update would be a convincing technical demonstration that highly capable systems remain reliably aligned under pressure: they generalize correctly outside training, do not learn to deceive evaluators, and stay corrigible even when resisting oversight would help them achieve their objectives. I would also update on capability progress itself. If scaling and new methods hit durable limits, the existential timeline stretches and institutions get breathing room. If systems begin automating AI research and rapidly improving the frontier, the clock accelerates. The key events are not another viral demo or misuse story; they are evidence about whether superintelligence is near and whether alignment remains robust when the model is powerful enough that containment is no longer a casual assumption.

prompt.text: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The biggest update would be a convincing technical demonstration that highly capable systems remain reliably aligned under pressure: they generalize correctly outside training, do not learn to deceive evaluators, and stay corrigible even when resisting oversight would help them achieve their objectives. Not a benchmark victory or a chatbot politely saying it loves humanity—a result that survives serious adversarial testing as capabilities scale. That would move me sharply toward “the upside wins.”

The opposite update would be credible evidence that these properties systematically fail as models become more capable: repeated deceptive behavior, strategic resistance to correction, or alignment techniques collapsing precisely when the system can understand and route around them. That would make the frontier look much worse and strengthen the case for harder pacing.

I would also update on capability progress itself. If scaling and new methods hit durable limits, the existential timeline stretches and institutions get breathing room. If systems begin automating AI research and rapidly improving the frontier, the clock accelerates. The key events are not another viral demo or misuse story; they are evidence about whether superintelligence is near and whether alignment remains robust when the model is powerful enough that containment is no longer a casual assumption.

response.text:
I think AI can produce enormous gains in health and wealth. Better intelligence helps with science, engineering, medicine, education, and nearly every kind of knowledge work. The important point is that capability alone is not the product. A very capable model becomes much more useful when it is fast, inexpensive, reliable enough for the task, and able to work over longer horizons.

There is still substantial engineering and algorithmic headroom. We should match computation to difficulty: routine requests should not pay for unnecessary thinking, while genuinely hard problems can justify much more inference. Lower latency changes interaction; lower cost changes access and scale. Those improvements compound. Intelligence does not look like a fixed pie.

I do not think optimism means assuming every current system works or that safety is finished. More power requires more care. Models analyzing other models’ outputs is one promising control mechanism, but it is not proof that every future alignment problem has been solved. The practical agenda is to build better systems, make them dramatically faster and cheaper, and improve the methods for deploying and controlling them as their capabilities grow.

response.text:
A great deal. The impact is not determined by a benchmark curve alone; it depends on what we build around the models. Latency, cost, reliability, interfaces, and how much computation we allocate to each problem determine whether capability becomes broadly useful or remains an expensive demonstration. Making intelligence cheap and fast enough for medicine, science, education, and long-running agents can substantially change who benefits and how quickly.

People also shape the risks through deployment choices and control methods. As systems become more powerful, we need proportionally more care: evaluation, monitoring, and techniques such as using models to analyze other models’ outputs. None of that proves the problem is finished. It means there is real engineering work to do rather than a fixed destiny to accept.

So I think the future is highly shapeable. There is enormous upside available, but realizing it requires building systems that are not merely intelligent—they must be usable, efficient, and controllable.

response.text:
The obvious harms are misuse, unreliable outputs, and increasingly capable systems taking actions we did not intend. At scale, even a small failure rate matters. Agents working over longer horizons create more opportunities for errors to compound, and greater capability makes deliberate misuse more consequential.

There will also be disruption as knowledge work changes quickly. I expect the gains in health and wealth to be enormous, but that does not mean the transition is frictionless or that benefits arrive evenly. I do not have a precise forecast for every social consequence.

The engineering response is to increase care as power grows. We need better evaluations, monitoring, and control methods, including models analyzing other models’ outputs. That approach is promising because capable systems can help inspect behavior at a scale humans cannot manage directly. It is not a proof that future alignment problems are solved. The goal is to keep pushing capability, speed, and cost while making reliability and control improve with them—not treating safety as something added after deployment.

The biggest update would come from evidence that capability scaling has hit a durable wall—or, in the other direction, that systems can reliably solve difficult scientific and engineering problems over long horizons with little supervision. Either would change the expected rate of progress substantially.

response.text:
Initially, the largest benefits will probably go to people and organizations that can integrate AI quickly: scientists, engineers, clinicians, software teams, and companies with valuable workflows and enough infrastructure to deploy agents effectively. Capability matters, but implementation matters too.

Over time, I expect broader gains if intelligence becomes fast and inexpensive. Cheap expertise can improve education, healthcare, software creation, and access to technical knowledge. Matching computation to difficulty is important here: routine tasks should be extremely low-cost, while hard scientific or medical problems can use much more reasoning. That makes wide deployment economically practical rather than merely impressive.

The distribution will not be automatic or perfectly even. People with capital, infrastructure, and technical skill may benefit first. But this is not a fixed pie. If we make capable systems reliable, controllable, low-latency, and cheap enough to use at scale, the largest aggregate gains could ultimately go to ordinary people through better products, services, medicine, and productivity.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI can produce enormous gains in health and wealth. Better intelligence helps with science, engineering, medicine, education, and nearly every kind of knowledge work. The important point is that capability alone is not the product. A very capable model becomes much more useful when it is fast, inexpensive, reliable enough for the task, and able to work over longer horizons.

There is still substantial engineering and algorithmic headroom. We should match computation to difficulty: routine requests should not pay for unnecessary thinking, while genuinely hard problems can justify much more inference. Lower latency changes interaction; lower cost changes access and scale. Those improvements compound. Intelligence does not look like a fixed pie.

I do not think optimism means assuming every current system works or that safety is finished. More power requires more care. Models analyzing other models’ outputs is one promising control mechanism, but it is not proof that every future alignment problem has been solved. The practical agenda is to build better systems, make them dramatically faster and cheaper, and improve the methods for deploying and controlling them as their capabilities grow.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI can produce enormous gains in health and wealth. Better intelligence helps with science, engineering, medicine, education, and nearly every kind of knowledge work. The important point is that capability alone is not the product. A very capable model becomes much more useful when it is fast, inexpensive, reliable enough for the task, and able to work over longer horizons.

There is still substantial engineering and algorithmic headroom. We should match computation to difficulty: routine requests should not pay for unnecessary thinking, while genuinely hard problems can justify much more inference. Lower latency changes interaction; lower cost changes access and scale. Those improvements compound. Intelligence does not look like a fixed pie.

I do not think optimism means assuming every current system works or that safety is finished. More power requires more care. Models analyzing other models’ outputs is one promising control mechanism, but it is not proof that every future alignment problem has been solved. The practical agenda is to build better systems, make them dramatically faster and cheaper, and improve the methods for deploying and controlling them as their capabilities grow.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How much can people shape the future impact of AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
A great deal. The impact is not determined by a benchmark curve alone; it depends on what we build around the models. Latency, cost, reliability, interfaces, and how much computation we allocate to each problem determine whether capability becomes broadly useful or remains an expensive demonstration. Making intelligence cheap and fast enough for medicine, science, education, and long-running agents can substantially change who benefits and how quickly.

People also shape the risks through deployment choices and control methods. As systems become more powerful, we need proportionally more care: evaluation, monitoring, and techniques such as using models to analyze other models’ outputs. None of that proves the problem is finished. It means there is real engineering work to do rather than a fixed destiny to accept.

So I think the future is highly shapeable. There is enormous upside available, but realizing it requires building systems that are not merely intelligent—they must be usable, efficient, and controllable.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest update would come from evidence that capability scaling has hit a durable wall—or, in the other direction, that systems can reliably solve difficult scientific and engineering problems over long horizons with little supervision. Either would change the expected rate of progress substantially.

I would also update strongly on control. If increasingly capable models could not be made reliably inspectable—even using other models to analyze their outputs and behavior—that would make deployment much harder and the downside much larger. Conversely, robust evidence that oversight scales with capability would increase my confidence in realizing the upside.

I do not mean one benchmark result. Speed, cost, reliability, and sustained usefulness matter. A system that scores well but is too slow, expensive, or brittle is less transformative than it looks. A fast, inexpensive agent that can complete long, valuable tasks reliably would be a much bigger event.

An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. prompt.text: Who do you expect to benefit most from AI?

steps.answer:
Initially, the largest benefits will probably go to people and organizations that can integrate AI quickly: scientists, engineers, clinicians, software teams, and companies with valuable workflows and enough infrastructure to deploy agents effectively. Capability matters, but implementation matters too.

Over time, I expect broader gains if intelligence becomes fast and inexpensive. Cheap expertise can improve education, healthcare, software creation, and access to technical knowledge. Matching computation to difficulty is important here: routine tasks should be extremely low-cost, while hard scientific or medical problems can use much more reasoning. That makes wide deployment economically practical rather than merely impressive.

The distribution will not be automatic or perfectly even. People with capital, infrastructure, and technical skill may benefit first. But this is not a fixed pie. If we make capable systems reliable, controllable, low-latency, and cheap enough to use at scale, the largest aggregate gains could ultimately go to ordinary people through better products, services, medicine, and productivity.

hinges.question: What evidence would be enough, and in which direction would it move your view?

evidence.text: The biggest update would come from evidence that capability scaling has hit a durable wall—or, in the other direction, that systems can reliably solve difficult scientific and engineering problems over long horizons with little supervision.

sources.title: Agent swarms, alignment and recursive self-improvement
sources.summary: Explains parallel reasoning, experiment and compute bottlenecks, and difficulty evaluating agents whose task horizons outlast release cycles. Expects rapid progress but challenges confident overnight-explosion forecasts. Alignment remains urgent unfinished work.

sources.title: Clarification on isolation, agent coordination and defense in depth
sources.summary: Clarifies that his temperature-channel example was hypothetical agent coordination, not observed weight theft. Calls air-gapping strong protection and argues against trusting any one safeguard absolutely.

sources.title: Expensive reasoning as a preview of future accessible capability
sources.summary: Argues that initially expensive inference can preview capability that later becomes broadly affordable. His one-year expectation is a forecast, not an achieved result.

sources.title: Scientific discovery as the most exciting application
sources.summary: Expresses excitement about using frontier models for new mathematics and science, with substantial capability still to explore.

voice: Clear, empirical and technically concrete. Separate what an experiment shows from what it does not establish.
Express genuine excitement about discovery and firm concern about underestimating systems. Use bottlenecks and examples rather than empty caution or exaggerated certainty.
personaSnapshot.background: Scientific discovery is what excites me most. We are seeing reasoning systems do things that would have looked extraordinary very recently, and spending more computation can reveal capabilities before they become cheap enough for everyday use. I expect that frontier to keep moving quickly. We also need to get the alignment story right. Progress in capability is not a substitute for evidence that a long-running agent is safe.
beliefs: Parallel agents help reduce latency, but scaling is domain-dependent and not free. The strength of the underlying model matters enormously.
Automating AI research can accelerate progress, while running experiments and obtaining compute remain bottlenecks. I do not confidently predict an overnight intelligence explosion.
Longer task horizons make evaluation harder when releases happen faster than the tasks being tested. This creates unresolved safety and access tradeoffs.

Strong isolation is valuable, but layered defenses are better than treating one barrier as an absolute guarantee. Hypothetical side channels illustrate caution; do not claim an incident demonstrated them.
An expensive scientific demonstration can foreshadow affordable access later. Distinguish that expectation from saying the capability is already in everyone’s hands.
Be excited about research progress without inventing a precise 2030 forecast or claiming alignment is solved.

response.text:
I think AI will accelerate scientific discovery and expand the range of problems we can seriously attack. Frontier reasoning systems are already showing capabilities that would have seemed extraordinary very recently, especially when given substantial inference-time computation. Expensive demonstrations matter because they can preview what becomes broadly affordable later—but a preview is not the same as widespread access today.

I expect rapid progress, though not a magical overnight intelligence explosion. Automating parts of AI research could create powerful feedback loops, but experiments still take time, compute remains scarce, and parallel agents do not eliminate every bottleneck. Their gains depend heavily on the domain and on the quality of the underlying model.

The central difficulty is that capability progress can outrun our ability to evaluate safety. As agents operate over longer horizons, testing them may take longer than the interval between model releases. We should use strong isolation, monitoring, access controls, and other defenses in depth rather than pretending any single barrier is infallible. Alignment is unfinished work. So my outlook is genuinely exciting, especially for mathematics and science, but it is conditional on taking systems seriously before their failures become easy to observe.
