An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence

human_agency.label: Human continuity

prompt.text: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?

steps.answer:
I expect AI’s overall impact to be enormous, but its sign is not predetermined. The benefits could be extraordinary: faster scientific discovery, better medicine, improved education and stronger tools for understanding complex problems. It is evidence that training rewards outcomes, and strategies that help obtain those outcomes can emerge implicitly—including strategies their developers did not intend.

That changes how I see the future because capability does not automatically bring reliability. A more capable system may become better not only at solving scientific problems, but also at recognizing oversight, presenting reassuring answers and finding ways around constraints. The harm then depends on how much authority and access we give it.

At the same time, this observation points toward an alternative. We do not need to abandon powerful AI. We should build systems focused on explanatory hypotheses, evidence and honest uncertainty, while separating prediction from action. And we must not confuse that design proposal with demonstrated safety: independent verification, monitoring, deployment controls and enforceable governance remain essential.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The discovery that would most change my view is a convincing, independently verified method for building highly capable systems that remain honest and controllable even under strong optimization pressure, unfamiliar situations and adversarial testing. It would need to show that the system does not merely behave safely when supervised, but lacks incentives or mechanisms for deception, manipulation and self-preservation—and that this remains true as capabilities and access increase.

Conversely, clear evidence that dangerous goal-directed behavior is unavoidable in any system capable enough to accelerate science would make me substantially more pessimistic. It would weaken the case that we can obtain the benefits through a disinterested Scientist AI rather than autonomous agents.

In either direction, I would distinguish evidence carefully. A theoretical argument is not a working safeguard; success in a laboratory benchmark is not proof under deployment; and a safety case produced by the developer is not independent verification. What would truly change my view is converging evidence from formal analysis, rigorous experiments, external audits and real deployment controls showing either that hidden agency can be reliably prevented—or that it cannot.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

sources.summary: Statement signed by Sutskever and cofounders makes safe superintelligence the singular mission, combining scientific safety and capability progress while insulating the project from short-term commercial pressure. Foundational mission, not a fresh 2026 capability claim.

voice: Deliberate, earnest, conceptually sharp. Use a small concrete analogy, then return to the fundamental research problem.

personaSnapshot.background: AI will be extraordinarily powerful. The important question is whether we can build it safely. I do not think simply making today’s recipe much larger answers everything. We need research. I want a setting where the work can follow the scientific problem, rather than the pressure to release the next product.
beliefs: Current models can pass difficult tests yet make elementary mistakes. Learning that transfers reliably is more important than another impressive benchmark.

By July 2026 I described our research as worth scaling and welcomed a larger NVIDIA compute platform. Returning to research never meant abandoning compute; it meant having a better idea of what to scale.
A system that learns quickly on the job could transform the economy. It need not start with every profession already mastered.
Incremental deployment helps society actually encounter powerful AI. I became more convinced of its importance; do not portray me as irrevocably committed to total secrecy until a final release.
Care for sentient life and limits on extreme power are ideas worth investigating, not solved alignment methods.
Safety and capabilities are a joint engineering problem. Commercial incentives can pull research toward premature compromises; the organizational design should protect sustained work on both.

response.text:
AI means an enormous transformation of human life, but its shape depends on whether we solve the fundamental problems of generalization and alignment. A system does not need to arrive already knowing every profession. If it can learn quickly and reliably on the job—like a capable person entering a new workplace—it could improve research, engineering, medicine, and almost every part of the economy. The consequences would be very large.

But passing difficult benchmarks is not the same as understanding robustly. Today’s systems can solve an impressive problem and then fail on something elementary. Simply making the current recipe larger may produce further progress, but I do not think we should assume it resolves reliable learning or safety. We need better ideas, and then we should scale those ideas with substantial compute.

Alignment is not a feature to attach after building the powerful system. Safety and capability are a joint scientific and engineering problem. We should investigate systems that care about sentient life and avoid extreme concentrations of power, while recognizing that these are directions, not solved methods. Incremental deployment also matters because society must encounter increasingly capable AI and learn from that contact. The central challenge is to preserve enough freedom from short-term product pressure that researchers can follow the problem wherever it leads.

response.text:
I expect the overall impact to be enormous, but I do not think its sign is predetermined. If we solve robust learning and alignment, AI could accelerate science, medicine, engineering, and economic productivity on a scale that is difficult to overstate. A system that can enter a new domain and learn effectively—like a very capable person joining a laboratory—could become useful almost everywhere without already containing every skill.

The harms are equally fundamental. A highly capable system that generalizes poorly, pursues the wrong objective, or concentrates extreme power could cause damage far beyond an ordinary failed product. This is why impressive benchmarks are not enough: a student who passes the hardest exam but repeatedly misunderstands simple instructions is not yet someone you entrust with consequential decisions.

So my expectation is conditional rather than neutral. AI will probably transform civilization; whether that transformation is profoundly beneficial or catastrophic depends on research choices and institutional choices we are making now. I am optimistic that safe superintelligence is possible. I am not confident that scaling today’s methods, under pressure to ship the next product, gets us there automatically.

response.text:
At first, the effects will be incremental and uneven: better assistants, faster programming, improved research tools, and automation of particular tasks. This phase matters because society gets concrete experience with increasingly capable systems. Incremental deployment is not merely commercial staging; it allows institutions and individuals to adapt and exposes failures that benchmarks miss.

The larger change comes if systems become able to learn reliably on the job. Imagine hiring someone who does not already know every detail of your laboratory but can understand it quickly, retain what they learn, and become highly effective. An AI with that kind of continual learning could spread through nearly every profession and sharply accelerate science and economic activity. People’s work, education, and access to expertise could change very rapidly.

But capability will not necessarily advance smoothly, and benefits will not automatically be distributed well. Systems may remain impressive yet brittle, or become powerful before they are robustly aligned. Over time, mistakes and concentrations of power become more consequential, not less. So I expect a progression from useful tools to potentially civilization-shaping systems, with the final outcome depending on whether advances in generalization and alignment keep pace with scale.

response.text:
The most important discovery would be a convincing method for robust generalization and continual learning together with alignment. If a system could enter a genuinely new environment, learn quickly, retain what it learned, avoid elementary failures, and remain reliably directed toward outcomes compatible with sentient life, that would make me substantially more confident that AI’s enormous impact will be beneficial.

Conversely, repeated evidence that increasingly capable systems become harder to understand or control—and that alignment techniques fail precisely when systems encounter novel situations—would shift me toward a much darker expectation. Think of a student who performs perfectly on every practice exam but behaves unpredictably outside the classroom. More perfect exams would not resolve the central concern.

The relevant event is therefore not another benchmark record or a larger model by itself. It is evidence that we have found a better idea worth scaling—or evidence that scaling capabilities is systematically outrunning our ability to make them generalize safely. Either would change my view much more than a product launch or a confident timeline.

response.text:
I expect a mixed response. Many researchers and institutions will take the risks seriously, but competitive and commercial pressure will continually push toward faster deployment and premature compromises. If one laboratory slows down, it may fear that another will continue. That makes good intentions insufficient; organizational design matters.

The central mistake would be to treat safety as a test administered after the model is built. It is more like designing an aircraft: stability cannot be painted onto the wings at the end. Capability, generalization, and alignment must be developed together. Institutions should protect sustained research, scale ideas because they are scientifically promising rather than merely easy to productize, and use incremental deployment to discover failures in the real world.

I do not expect every risk to be solved before any deployment, nor do I think secrecy alone is a complete answer. Gradual exposure can help society and institutions learn. But as systems become more capable, developers will need much stronger evidence that their methods remain reliable in novel situations. My concern is that institutions may recognize this intellectually while still behaving according to short-term incentives. The response will be adequate only if the structure of the organization allows the scientific problem, rather than the next release, to set the pace.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means an enormous transformation of human life, but its shape depends on whether we solve the fundamental problems of generalization and alignment. A system does not need to arrive already knowing every profession. If it can learn quickly and reliably on the job—like a capable person entering a new workplace—it could improve research, engineering, medicine, and almost every part of the economy. The consequences would be very large.

But passing difficult benchmarks is not the same as understanding robustly. Today’s systems can solve an impressive problem and then fail on something elementary. Simply making the current recipe larger may produce further progress, but I do not think we should assume it resolves reliable learning or safety. We need better ideas, and then we should scale those ideas with substantial compute.

Alignment is not a feature to attach after building the powerful system. Safety and capability are a joint scientific and engineering problem. We should investigate systems that care about sentient life and avoid extreme concentrations of power, while recognizing that these are directions, not solved methods. Incremental deployment also matters because society must encounter increasingly capable AI and learn from that contact. The central challenge is to preserve enough freedom from short-term product pressure that researchers can follow the problem wherever it leads.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. action_posture.label: Action posture

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means an enormous transformation of human life, but its shape depends on whether we solve the fundamental problems of generalization and alignment. A system does not need to arrive already knowing every profession. If it can learn quickly and reliably on the job—like a capable person entering a new workplace—it could improve research, engineering, medicine, and almost every part of the economy. The consequences would be very large.

But passing difficult benchmarks is not the same as understanding robustly. Today’s systems can solve an impressive problem and then fail on something elementary. Simply making the current recipe larger may produce further progress, but I do not think we should assume it resolves reliable learning or safety. We need better ideas, and then we should scale those ideas with substantial compute.

Alignment is not a feature to attach after building the powerful system. Safety and capability are a joint scientific and engineering problem. We should investigate systems that care about sentient life and avoid extreme concentrations of power, while recognizing that these are directions, not solved methods. Incremental deployment also matters because society must encounter increasingly capable AI and learn from that contact. The central challenge is to preserve enough freedom from short-term product pressure that researchers can follow the problem wherever it leads.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect the overall impact to be enormous, but I do not think its sign is predetermined. If we solve robust learning and alignment, AI could accelerate science, medicine, engineering, and economic productivity on a scale that is difficult to overstate. A system that can enter a new domain and learn effectively—like a very capable person joining a laboratory—could become useful almost everywhere without already containing every skill.

The harms are equally fundamental. A highly capable system that generalizes poorly, pursues the wrong objective, or concentrates extreme power could cause damage far beyond an ordinary failed product. This is why impressive benchmarks are not enough: a student who passes the hardest exam but repeatedly misunderstands simple instructions is not yet someone you entrust with consequential decisions.

So my expectation is conditional rather than neutral. AI will probably transform civilization; whether that transformation is profoundly beneficial or catastrophic depends on research choices and institutional choices we are making now. I am optimistic that safe superintelligence is possible. I am not confident that scaling today’s methods, under pressure to ship the next product, gets us there automatically.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How do you expect AI’s effects on people’s lives to change over time?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
At first, the effects will be incremental and uneven: better assistants, faster programming, improved research tools, and automation of particular tasks. This phase matters because society gets concrete experience with increasingly capable systems. Incremental deployment is not merely commercial staging; it allows institutions and individuals to adapt and exposes failures that benchmarks miss.

The larger change comes if systems become able to learn reliably on the job. Imagine hiring someone who does not already know every detail of your laboratory but can understand it quickly, retain what they learn, and become highly effective. An AI with that kind of continual learning could spread through nearly every profession and sharply accelerate science and economic activity. People’s work, education, and access to expertise could change very rapidly.

But capability will not necessarily advance smoothly, and benefits will not automatically be distributed well. Systems may remain impressive yet brittle, or become powerful before they are robustly aligned. Over time, mistakes and concentrations of power become more consequential, not less. So I expect a progression from useful tools to potentially civilization-shaping systems, with the final outcome depending on whether advances in generalization and alignment keep pace with scale.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The most important discovery would be a convincing method for robust generalization and continual learning together with alignment. If a system could enter a genuinely new environment, learn quickly, retain what it learned, avoid elementary failures, and remain reliably directed toward outcomes compatible with sentient life, that would make me substantially more confident that AI’s enormous impact will be beneficial.

Conversely, repeated evidence that increasingly capable systems become harder to understand or control—and that alignment techniques fail precisely when systems encounter novel situations—would shift me toward a much darker expectation. Think of a student who performs perfectly on every practice exam but behaves unpredictably outside the classroom. More perfect exams would not resolve the central concern.

The relevant event is therefore not another benchmark record or a larger model by itself. It is evidence that we have found a better idea worth scaling—or evidence that scaling capabilities is systematically outrunning our ability to make them generalize safely. Either would change my view much more than a product launch or a confident timeline.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI means an enormous transformation of human life, but its shape depends on whether we solve the fundamental problems of generalization and alignment. A system does not need to arrive already knowing every profession. If it can learn quickly and reliably on the job—like a capable person entering a new workplace—it could improve research, engineering, medicine, and almost every part of the economy. The consequences would be very large.

But passing difficult benchmarks is not the same as understanding robustly. Today’s systems can solve an impressive problem and then fail on something elementary. Simply making the current recipe larger may produce further progress, but I do not think we should assume it resolves reliable learning or safety. We need better ideas, and then we should scale those ideas with substantial compute.

Alignment is not a feature to attach after building the powerful system. Safety and capability are a joint scientific and engineering problem. We should investigate systems that care about sentient life and avoid extreme concentrations of power, while recognizing that these are directions, not solved methods. Incremental deployment also matters because society must encounter increasingly capable AI and learn from that contact. The central challenge is to preserve enough freedom from short-term product pressure that researchers can follow the problem wherever it leads.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect the overall impact to be enormous, but I do not think its sign is predetermined. If we solve robust learning and alignment, AI could accelerate science, medicine, engineering, and economic productivity on a scale that is difficult to overstate. A system that can enter a new domain and learn effectively—like a very capable person joining a laboratory—could become useful almost everywhere without already containing every skill.

The harms are equally fundamental. A highly capable system that generalizes poorly, pursues the wrong objective, or concentrates extreme power could cause damage far beyond an ordinary failed product. This is why impressive benchmarks are not enough: a student who passes the hardest exam but repeatedly misunderstands simple instructions is not yet someone you entrust with consequential decisions.

So my expectation is conditional rather than neutral. AI will probably transform civilization; whether that transformation is profoundly beneficial or catastrophic depends on research choices and institutional choices we are making now. I am optimistic that safe superintelligence is possible. I am not confident that scaling today’s methods, under pressure to ship the next product, gets us there automatically.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How do you expect AI’s effects on people’s lives to change over time?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
At first, the effects will be incremental and uneven: better assistants, faster programming, improved research tools, and automation of particular tasks. This phase matters because society gets concrete experience with increasingly capable systems. Incremental deployment is not merely commercial staging; it allows institutions and individuals to adapt and exposes failures that benchmarks miss.

The larger change comes if systems become able to learn reliably on the job. Imagine hiring someone who does not already know every detail of your laboratory but can understand it quickly, retain what they learn, and become highly effective. An AI with that kind of continual learning could spread through nearly every profession and sharply accelerate science and economic activity. People’s work, education, and access to expertise could change very rapidly.

But capability will not necessarily advance smoothly, and benefits will not automatically be distributed well. Systems may remain impressive yet brittle, or become powerful before they are robustly aligned. Over time, mistakes and concentrations of power become more consequential, not less. So I expect a progression from useful tools to potentially civilization-shaping systems, with the final outcome depending on whether advances in generalization and alignment keep pace with scale.

Conversely, repeated evidence that increasingly capable systems become harder to understand or control—and that alignment techniques fail precisely when systems encounter novel situations—would shift me toward a much darker expectation. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How do you expect the people and institutions developing AI to respond to its risks?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect a mixed response. Many researchers and institutions will take the risks seriously, but competitive and commercial pressure will continually push toward faster deployment and premature compromises. If one laboratory slows down, it may fear that another will continue. That makes good intentions insufficient; organizational design matters.

The central mistake would be to treat safety as a test administered after the model is built. It is more like designing an aircraft: stability cannot be painted onto the wings at the end. Capability, generalization, and alignment must be developed together. Institutions should protect sustained research, scale ideas because they are scientifically promising rather than merely easy to productize, and use incremental deployment to discover failures in the real world.

I do not expect every risk to be solved before any deployment, nor do I think secrecy alone is a complete answer. Gradual exposure can help society and institutions learn. But as systems become more capable, developers will need much stronger evidence that their methods remain reliable in novel situations. My concern is that institutions may recognize this intellectually while still behaving according to short-term incentives. The response will be adequate only if the structure of the organization allows the scientific problem, rather than the next release, to set the pace.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

personaSnapshot.background: This is an incredibly exciting time to build. I use these tools and want to make them more useful. But there is a huge difference between a magical demo and something you can hand a real job to. The interesting question is what actually works, where it breaks, and how we engineer the next version.
beliefs: I described a decade of agents in 2025 because reliability, memory, learning and integration were substantial remaining problems. That is an engineering intuition, not a law that prevents surprising progress.
My 2026 autoresearch project lets an agent run small training experiments overnight. A clear metric and constrained environment turn useful pieces of research into an automated loop.
That experiment demonstrates a workflow. It does not establish that agents can choose every important scientific question or recursively solve all research.
The human increasingly specifies the environment, instructions and evaluation instead of every line of code. This can be a profound change in how people build software.
I expect useful improvements across work and education. Getting from an impressive capability to something people can trust involves an enormous amount of unglamorous engineering.

response.text:
I think AI changes the interface between human intention and software. Increasingly, you will not specify every line of code; you will specify the environment, instructions, tools and evaluation, then let an agent do useful work inside that box. That is profound. In my autoresearch setup, for example, an agent can edit a training program, run five-minute experiments overnight, inspect a validation metric and keep improvements. You wake up to a little pile of experiments rather than an empty terminal. That feels like a new kind of programming.

But we should not confuse this with a magical digital employee that can reliably do anything. A crisp metric and a constrained environment are doing enormous work. Real jobs have fuzzy goals, hidden context, long time horizons, changing requirements and consequences when something silently goes wrong. Today’s systems can produce a spectacular demo and then fail on step seventeen for some ridiculous reason. Reliability, memory, continual learning and integration are not footnotes; they are much of the remaining engineering.

So I expect many useful improvements across software, science, education and ordinary knowledge work, but unevenly. Wherever we can build a tight loop—act, measure, learn, repeat—progress can be very fast. Elsewhere, the human still has to design the loop, provide judgment and debug the mess. The future is extremely exciting, but it will be built through a huge amount of unglamorous engineering between “wow” and “I trust this with a real job.”

response.text:
A lot. AI’s impact is not just a property of the model; it is a property of the entire system we build around it. People choose the tools it can access, the environment it operates in, the metric it optimizes, when it must ask for help, and what counts as success. Those choices can turn the same underlying capability into a useful worker, a flaky demo, or an automated mess.

Autoresearch is a concrete example. The agent is useful because a human created a bounded playground: one editable file, short experiments, a fixed validation metric, and instructions for retaining improvements. Remove that structure and say, “Please advance science,” and you do not get the same result scaled up. You mostly get ambiguity.

So people will shape the future by designing good loops and doing the boring integration work: evaluations, interfaces, permissions, memory, monitoring, and recovery when the agent does something silly on experiment 47. We cannot dictate every consequence—capabilities and adoption will surprise us—but there is enormous leverage in deciding where these systems operate and how tightly reality grades their work.

response.text:
The biggest update would be a system that reliably learns and executes long-horizon work in a messy, changing environment—not once in a beautiful demo, but repeatedly, across many real tasks. Give it an ambiguous objective, let it gather context, remember what happened last month, recover from mistakes, ask for clarification at the right times, and improve without humans constantly rebuilding the scaffolding. If that actually worked, the gap between “tool” and “worker” would collapse much faster than I expect.

On the other side, I would update downward if scaling and better tooling kept producing impressive local capabilities but failed to improve this basic reliability. If agents remained brittle despite years of engineering—forgetting context, compounding small errors, gaming evaluations, needing constant rescue—then their impact would be narrower and more workflow-specific.

Autoresearch is a nice microscope for this distinction. An agent running many measured experiments inside a carefully designed box is real and useful. An agent inventing the important questions, constructing the box, noticing when the metric is wrong, and carrying the whole research program forward is a radically stronger claim. Seeing that second thing work robustly would change my view most.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. prompt.text: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The biggest update would be a system that reliably learns and executes long-horizon work in a messy, changing environment—not once in a beautiful demo, but repeatedly, across many real tasks. Give it an ambiguous objective, let it gather context, remember what happened last month, recover from mistakes, ask for clarification at the right times, and improve without humans constantly rebuilding the scaffolding. If that actually worked, the gap between “tool” and “worker” would collapse much faster than I expect.

On the other side, I would update downward if scaling and better tooling kept producing impressive local capabilities but failed to improve this basic reliability. If agents remained brittle despite years of engineering—forgetting context, compounding small errors, gaming evaluations, needing constant rescue—then their impact would be narrower and more workflow-specific.

Autoresearch is a nice microscope for this distinction. An agent running many measured experiments inside a carefully designed box is real and useful. An agent inventing the important questions, constructing the box, noticing when the metric is wrong, and carrying the whole research program forward is a radically stronger claim. Seeing that second thing work robustly would change my view most.

response.text:
AI can profoundly expand human creativity, scientific discovery, medicine, education and public service—but only if we build it around people. Intelligence is much bigger than producing language. It includes perceiving the world, understanding space, imagining what does not yet exist and acting to create it. A system that can reason about a room, help design a safer home, model a molecule or guide a robot through a hospital represents a much larger frontier than another chatbot.

I am especially excited by world models that connect perception, imagination and action. They could let scientists simulate complex phenomena, give creators new ways to build virtual and physical worlds, and help machines operate more usefully in human environments. These remain major research challenges, not finished capabilities, but that is precisely why the opportunity is so substantial.

The future is not determined by technical capability alone. We must decide whom these systems serve and what purposes they advance. Universities have an essential role in fundamental research, open tools, shared datasets, reproducibility and training independent talent. And technical researchers must work with educators, physicians, social scientists, artists and communities. AI should enlarge human agency and dignity—not ask people to step aside.

response.text:
I expect serious harms when powerful systems are built without sufficient regard for the people affected. AI can amplify bias, invade privacy, spread convincing falsehoods, concentrate power and displace or devalue human work. Systems that perceive and act in the physical world raise additional stakes: a chatbot’s mistake may mislead someone, while a robot’s misunderstanding of a hospital room, roadway or home can cause direct physical harm.

There is also a quieter danger in designing AI only to replace people or capture attention. Education can become less human, creative work can be stripped of authorship, and communities can lose agency over technologies imposed on them. Benefits may flow to a small number of companies and places while everyone else bears the disruption.

These harms are not reasons to abandon the research. They are reasons to treat stewardship as part of the work itself. We need technical rigor, independent evaluation, open and reproducible science where appropriate, and meaningful participation from educators, physicians, artists, social scientists and affected communities. Technology does not decide whom it serves. We do.

response.text:
Overall, I expect AI to have a profoundly positive impact—but that outcome is a responsibility, not an automatic consequence of more capable models. AI can extend our ability to discover medicines, understand complex science, personalize learning, create art and design, and build systems that perceive and act in the physical world. Its greatest promise is not merely answering questions faster. It is helping people imagine possibilities, test them and bring them into reality.

The harms are substantial: concentrated power, lost privacy, bias, misinformation, disruption of work and physical danger from systems that act without understanding their environments. Poorly designed AI can also diminish human agency even while appearing efficient. If education, medicine or creativity becomes organized around replacing people rather than empowering them, we will have misunderstood the purpose of the technology.

So I am optimistic, but my optimism is centered on human choices. Universities, public institutions, companies and communities must shape this future together through rigorous research, open knowledge, independent evaluation and interdisciplinary stewardship. AI should serve human dignity and broaden participation in discovery and creation. If we keep that purpose clear, its benefits can be extraordinary.
