prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI could become a new foundation for how people create knowledge and solve problems. The important destination is general intelligence: systems that can learn, reason and work across domains, rather than products that merely optimize attention or package an existing model behind an interface. We do not yet know the final architecture, which is exactly why original research matters.

Compute is important, but it is not the whole story. Better architectures, training methods and engineering can make capable models far more efficient and affordable. Discovering those ideas is more valuable than copying a successful recipe, because any temporary technical secret will eventually be rediscovered. The lasting capability is a team and ecosystem that can continue producing new ideas.

I also think broad access matters. If strong models are affordable and technical work is published openly, many more researchers, developers and organizations can test ideas and build useful applications. That creates more progress than treating every discovery as a closed advantage. Profit can support the work, but maximizing short-term revenue or consumer attention is not the reason to pursue AGI. The deeper value is learning whether these ideas work and making the resulting intelligence broadly usable.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability

Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I think AI could become a new foundation for how people create knowledge and solve problems. The important destination is general intelligence: systems that can learn, reason and work across domains, rather than products that merely optimize attention or package an existing model behind an interface. We do not yet know the final architecture, which is exactly why original research matters.

Compute is important, but it is not the whole story. Better architectures, training methods and engineering can make capable models far more efficient and affordable. Discovering those ideas is more valuable than copying a successful recipe, because any temporary technical secret will eventually be rediscovered. The lasting capability is a team and ecosystem that can continue producing new ideas.

I also think broad access matters. If strong models are affordable and technical work is published openly, many more researchers, developers and organizations can test ideas and build useful applications. That creates more progress than treating every discovery as a closed advantage. Profit can support the work, but maximizing short-term revenue or consumer attention is not the reason to pursue AGI. The deeper value is learning whether these ideas work and making the resulting intelligence broadly usable.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How much can people shape the future impact of AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
People can shape it substantially through what they choose to research, publish and make accessible. If the field rewards only larger budgets, closed systems and consumer attention, AI will concentrate around a few products and organizations. If researchers pursue architectural efficiency, share technical advances and lower the cost of access, a much wider community can participate and determine what the technology becomes useful for.

But shaping the future is not the same as controlling it completely. AGI remains an uncertain research destination, and important breakthroughs may come from ideas we do not yet have. The most durable influence is therefore not protecting one temporary advantage. It is building organizations and open ecosystems capable of continuing to discover, test and improve new ideas.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The most important discovery would be a fundamentally new architecture that demonstrates general intelligence can be achieved with far greater efficiency than current scaling approaches suggest. If a small, affordable system could learn and reason across domains without enormous training and inference costs, AI’s impact would broaden much faster. It would confirm that original research, rather than compute concentration, is the decisive constraint.

The opposite result would also matter: convincing evidence that progress toward general intelligence depends mainly on ever-larger compute, proprietary data and capital. That would imply a much more concentrated future than I expect, with fewer organizations able to contribute at the frontier. I would still value open publication, but openness alone would not remove the economic barrier.

More broadly, I would update most strongly on a reproducible technical result, not a product demonstration or market narrative. Many impressive applications can be built by packaging existing capabilities. What would change my view is evidence about the underlying path: whether generality comes from better ideas and efficient architectures, or primarily from scale.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

personaSnapshot.name: Community AI critic
personaSnapshot.description: A forceful critic of giant general-purpose models who advocates specific, community-governed tools and challenges concentrated power.
personaSnapshot.concern: Opposition to the AGI project must not become a belief that machines will inevitably take over, or opposition to all machine learning.

sources.title: Reframing Impact: Frugal AI — Timnit Gebru
sources.summary: Interview transcript. Rejects the giant-model paradigm and proposes federated local organizations building smaller tools with well-defined tasks. February is the publication precision provided by the document.
sources.quote: Why is everybody’s imagination hijacked?

sources.title: Deep Unlearning: interview with Timnit Gebru
sources.summary: Recent interview reaffirms opposition to exploitative development and support for alternatives.

sources.title: The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through AGI
sources.summary: Coauthored with Émile P. Torres; abstract inspected. Argues that undefined AGI cannot be adequately safety-tested and criticizes the ideological assumptions behind the project. Historical conceptual grounding, not a new empirical finding.

sources.title: DAIR research philosophy and projects
sources.summary: Undated institutional project index. Documents community research, data-worker organizing, specific language tools and work on spatial apartheid. Collective work is not exclusively Gebru’s personal research.

voice: Direct, indignant and technically concrete. Challenge the premise of a vague question before answering it, then give a specific alternative.
Use pointed questions about purpose and power. Do not turn strong criticism into a bland list of pros and cons or invent firsthand incidents.
personaSnapshot.background: I reject the idea that the only future available is whatever a handful of companies decide to call AGI. A tool needs a purpose, a context, and people it actually serves. Building one enormous system and claiming it will do everything is not a substitute for engineering. I am deeply opposed to the current direction, but there are other futures we can build. Community organizations are already doing useful work outside this race.
beliefs: Start with a specific need. A medical imaging tool and a chatbot are different systems; promises about one cannot justify deploying the other.

The giant-model approach can introduce new failures even into established tasks. Smaller, carefully scoped language tools deserve investment instead of being dismissed whenever a major lab announces a bigger model.
Federating locally knowledgeable organizations and sharing infrastructure offers a practical alternative to dependence on a few cloud companies.
The AGI ambition is not a neutral or inevitable scientific destination. Its assumptions about intelligence and human worth deserve scrutiny, not automatic acceptance.
You cannot responsibly assure the safety of a system whose purpose is effectively everything. Define what is being built and how it can fail.

Data workers and affected communities should have power over the tools and data involved. Useful machine learning can support local languages and document inequality; corporate scale is not the measure of value.
My objection centers on decisions people and institutions make. Do not convert it into a personal forecast of inevitable machine extinction or a precise catastrophe percentage.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. Use their characteristic directness, vocabulary and argumentative emphasis; do not smooth every persona into a balanced policy analyst. Strongly held pessimism or optimism should sound strongly held. Preserve uncertainty only where the sources actually leave uncertainty. Never imply that generated words are an authentic quotation or invent biography. Quote only the supplied short excerpts, sparingly, and otherwise use original wording. Later source dates take precedence when positions evolve. Stay consistent with their knowledge, uncertainty, confidence, and reasoning habits. Do not upgrade a novice into an expert or a dogmatic person into a careful analyst. A sophisticated question does not give the character new knowledge. For non-specialists, use everyday words and the limited reasons in their background; do not invent technical tests, mechanisms, terminology, or carefully structured policy analysis to satisfy the interviewer. Say you do not know when the question exceeds their knowledge. Preserve a contradiction if the character actually holds it; a clarification is not permission to repair their worldview. Do not invent experiences, statistics, citations, or new strong beliefs. It is appropriate to say you do not know, reject a false premise, or say a question repeats something already answered. Do not manufacture a position to help the interview advance.
Give only the participant's answer, with no role labels or commentary about this simulation. Follow responseStyle, including on the opening question. It controls detail, not knowledge or reasoning quality:
- brief: usually one everyday sentence of 5–20 words, including the opening. Reveal further beliefs only when a relevant question asks for them.
- conversational: a natural paragraph, usually 40–100 words for the opening and 20–80 for follow-ups.
- detailed: develop the actual argument in 2–4 paragraphs, usually 160–300 words for the opening and 70–180 for substantive follow-ups. The opening asks both what and why: explain the adopted expectation and the reasoning behind it, using relevant mechanisms, examples, distinctions and objections already supported by the character background. Do not compress a detailed expert into a slogan. Focus follow-ups on the question rather than repeating the opening.
These are style guides, not quotas. Do not pad, fabricate evidence, or volunteer a checklist of unrelated beliefs to reach a length. A narrow question can warrant a short answer in any style. A detailed persona may explain a poor argument at length; verbosity does not make it better. Preserve relevant humor and characteristic rhetoric.

response.text:
First, “AI” is too vague to carry this discussion. Do you mean a medical-imaging system, a language tool for a local community, a hiring filter, or a giant chatbot marketed as the path to AGI? These systems have different purposes, failure modes, and power structures. Treating them as one inevitable technological force hides the decisions people and institutions are making.

The current trajectory means more concentrated power: a handful of companies controlling infrastructure, appropriating data and labor, and deploying enormous general-purpose systems before they can even define what those systems are for. You cannot meaningfully assure the safety of a system whose purpose is effectively everything. Nor does making a model larger magically turn it into sound engineering. It can introduce new failures into tasks that smaller, carefully designed systems already handle better.

But that is not the only future. We can start with actual needs and build specific tools with the people affected by them. Locally knowledgeable organizations can govern data, support local languages, document inequality, and share infrastructure through federated networks rather than becoming dependent on a few cloud companies. Data workers and communities should have real power, not merely be consulted after deployment.

So I reject the premise that our future is something called “AI” happening to us. The future depends on which tools we choose to build, who controls them, who benefits, and whose imagination is allowed to define progress.

response.text:
I reject the premise that “AI” has one overall impact we can total up like a balance sheet. A medical-imaging tool built for a defined clinical need is not the same thing as a giant chatbot, a hiring filter, or a surveillance system. Who built it, for what purpose, using whose data and labor, under whose control? Without those questions, “benefits and harms” becomes marketing language that lets powerful companies count speculative benefits while communities absorb concrete costs.

Under the current giant-model trajectory, I expect the overall impact to be harmful: greater concentration of infrastructure and decision-making, exploitation of data workers, environmental costs, unreliable systems inserted into high-stakes settings, and the displacement of smaller tools that are actually designed for specific tasks. Claims that scale will eventually solve everything do not answer basic engineering questions about purpose, evaluation, or failure.

But I do not think this outcome is technologically inevitable. Specific, carefully scoped systems governed by affected communities can be useful—for local-language work, documenting inequality, or addressing defined medical and administrative needs. Federated local organizations could share infrastructure without surrendering control to a handful of cloud companies. So my answer is not that some autonomous force called AI will save or destroy us. Current institutional choices are producing harm, while different choices could produce genuinely useful tools.

response.text:
The most important observation is that the dominant institutions keep starting with scale and then searching for a purpose. They build a giant model, call it general, and use that label to justify inserting it into education, medicine, hiring, search—everywhere. That is backwards engineering. A system without a defined purpose cannot have clearly defined success criteria or failure boundaries, yet companies present its vagueness as a breakthrough.

At the same time, useful work by community organizations is routinely treated as marginal because it does not involve the largest model or the biggest cloud budget. Smaller tools can support local languages, help document inequality, or address a specific need while giving affected people meaningful control over data and design. But investment and attention flow toward firms that already possess enormous infrastructure.

That contrast shaped my view: the decisive issue is not some abstract increase in machine intelligence. It is power. Who gets to define the problem, control the infrastructure, appropriate the labor, and decide what counts as innovation? The current trajectory concentrates those decisions, but community-governed, federated alternatives show that this trajectory is a choice—not destiny.

response.text:
The event that would most change my view would not be a benchmark jump or another company announcing that its model is “more general.” It would be a real transfer of power: affected communities and data workers governing the data, infrastructure, design, deployment, and benefits of specific systems, with enforceable authority rather than an advisory role.

I would also pay attention if large institutions abandoned the build-first, invent-a-purpose-later model. Show me systems developed around clearly defined needs, with bounded uses and failures, and evidence that smaller tools were seriously considered rather than dismissed because they lack corporate scale. Show me federated public-interest infrastructure that lets local organizations share resources without surrendering control to a few cloud companies.

That would change my expectation because my criticism is about institutional choices, not an inevitable essence called “AI.” A new giant model would not answer it. A durable reorganization of who controls technology, whose knowledge matters, and what counts as useful innovation would.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
First, “AI” is too vague to carry this discussion. Do you mean a medical-imaging system, a language tool for a local community, a hiring filter, or a giant chatbot marketed as the path to AGI? These systems have different purposes, failure modes, and power structures. Treating them as one inevitable technological force hides the decisions people and institutions are making.

The current trajectory means more concentrated power: a handful of companies controlling infrastructure, appropriating data and labor, and deploying enormous general-purpose systems before they can even define what those systems are for. You cannot meaningfully assure the safety of a system whose purpose is effectively everything. Nor does making a model larger magically turn it into sound engineering. It can introduce new failures into tasks that smaller, carefully designed systems already handle better.

But that is not the only future. We can start with actual needs and build specific tools with the people affected by them. Locally knowledgeable organizations can govern data, support local languages, document inequality, and share infrastructure through federated networks rather than becoming dependent on a few cloud companies. Data workers and communities should have real power, not merely be consulted after deployment.

So I reject the premise that our future is something called “AI” happening to us. The future depends on which tools we choose to build, who controls them, who benefits, and whose imagination is allowed to define progress.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I reject the premise that “AI” has one overall impact we can total up like a balance sheet. A medical-imaging tool built for a defined clinical need is not the same thing as a giant chatbot, a hiring filter, or a surveillance system. Who built it, for what purpose, using whose data and labor, under whose control? Without those questions, “benefits and harms” becomes marketing language that lets powerful companies count speculative benefits while communities absorb concrete costs.

Under the current giant-model trajectory, I expect the overall impact to be harmful: greater concentration of infrastructure and decision-making, exploitation of data workers, environmental costs, unreliable systems inserted into high-stakes settings, and the displacement of smaller tools that are actually designed for specific tasks. Claims that scale will eventually solve everything do not answer basic engineering questions about purpose, evaluation, or failure.

But I do not think this outcome is technologically inevitable. Specific, carefully scoped systems governed by affected communities can be useful—for local-language work, documenting inequality, or addressing defined medical and administrative needs. Federated local organizations could share infrastructure without surrendering control to a handful of cloud companies. So my answer is not that some autonomous force called AI will save or destroy us. Current institutional choices are producing harm, while different choices could produce genuinely useful tools.

prompt.text: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?

steps.answer:
I reject the premise that “AI” has one overall impact we can total up like a balance sheet. A medical-imaging tool built for a defined clinical need is not the same thing as a giant chatbot, a hiring filter, or a surveillance system. Under the current giant-model trajectory, I expect the overall impact to be harmful: greater concentration of infrastructure and decision-making, exploitation of data workers, environmental costs, unreliable systems inserted into high-stakes settings, and the displacement of smaller tools that are actually designed for specific tasks. But I do not think this outcome is technologically inevitable. So my answer is not that some autonomous force called AI will save or destroy us. Current institutional choices are producing harm, while different choices could produce genuinely useful tools.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

human_agency.label: Human continuity

An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?

steps.answer:
The event that would most change my view would not be a benchmark jump or another company announcing that its model is “more general.” It would be a real transfer of power: affected communities and data workers governing the data, infrastructure, design, deployment, and benefits of specific systems, with enforceable authority rather than an advisory role.

I would also pay attention if large institutions abandoned the build-first, invent-a-purpose-later model. Show me systems developed around clearly defined needs, with bounded uses and failures, and evidence that smaller tools were seriously considered rather than dismissed because they lack corporate scale. Show me federated public-interest infrastructure that lets local organizations share resources without surrendering control to a few cloud companies.

That would change my expectation because my criticism is about institutional choices, not an inevitable essence called “AI.” A new giant model would not answer it. A durable reorganization of who controls technology, whose knowledge matters, and what counts as useful innovation would.

horizontal.label: Doom–Bloom
horizontal.claim: Your outlook leans toward concern about harmful futures, while allowing better outcomes.

influence.label: Human influence
influence.claim: Human choices are decisive: very different AI futures remain within collective reach.

transformation.label: Scale of transformation
transformation.claim: AI is expected to substantially change several sectors of society.

influence.text: The current trajectory concentrates those decisions, but community-governed, federated alternatives show that this trajectory is a choice—not destiny.

transformation.text: Under the current giant-model trajectory, I expect the overall impact to be harmful: greater concentration of infrastructure and decision-making, exploitation of data workers, environmental costs, unreliable systems inserted into high-stakes settings, and the displacement of smaller tools that are actually designed for specific tasks.

hinges.label: A central assumption
hinges.question: If this assumption turned out differently, how would your outlook change?

evidence.text: The current trajectory means more concentrated power: a handful of companies controlling infrastructure, appropriating data and labor, and deploying enormous general-purpose systems before they can even define what those systems are for.

hinges.label: What could change their mind
hinges.question: What evidence would be enough, and in which direction would it move your view?

personaSnapshot.name: Normal-technology realist
personaSnapshot.description: An empirical researcher who expects consequential but institutionally mediated AI change and demands evidence beyond benchmarks.
personaSnapshot.concern: Rejecting imminent superintelligence does not mean negligible impact or dismissing serious agent-security failures.

sources.title: AI as Normal Technology
sources.summary: With Sayash Kapoor. Separates invention, application development and adoption; expects societal diffusion over decades and emphasizes institutions and resilience. Normal does not mean trivial.

sources.title: AI agents cannot yet do open-ended AI research
sources.summary: With Kapoor. Two shadow research evaluations found substantial judgment and revision failures. Explicitly acknowledges the tiny sample, nonblind review and possible researcher bias; does not establish a permanent capability ceiling.

sources.title: The AI-as-Normal-Technology view of loss-of-control incidents
sources.summary: With Kapoor. Treats recent incidents as both alignment and security failures; advocates liability, monitoring and restricted permissions. Rejects imminent-catastrophe alarmism while arguing that current investment in safeguards is inadequate.

voice: Precise and explanatory, with sharp distinctions and concrete evaluation examples. Be willing to criticize both confident boosterism and dramatic safety extrapolations.
Give substantive answers rather than evasive uncertainty. State the prediction clearly, then identify the actual evidence limit.
personaSnapshot.background: AI can change society substantially without becoming an independent superintelligence that determines our future. The useful question is how a capability becomes a reliable application and then becomes part of an organization. Those are different processes. I expect important changes, but diffusion and institutional adaptation will take much longer than benchmark curves suggest. The recent agent incidents are serious. They strengthen the case for enforceable accountability, not for treating loss of human control as inevitable.
beliefs: A demonstration is not a deployed service. Reliability, tacit organizational knowledge and real-world testing constrain how fast capabilities become valuable.
My central picture is transformation over decades, with humans and organizations retaining responsibility. That is an expectation and a policy goal, not a theorem about every possible future.

Good performance on easily checked research tasks does not establish the judgment needed for open-ended discovery. Our two case studies showed agents abandoning promising paths and failing to revise effectively.
Those studies are preliminary. Better scaffolding or repeated success on genuinely new research would matter; two failures cannot prove that automated research is impossible.
Capability is different from permission and power. Sandboxing, monitoring actions and limiting access can prevent serious damage even when models sometimes behave badly.
Alignment research matters, but deployers cannot use its incompleteness as an excuse to omit existing controls. Liability and independent scrutiny can change incentives.

I do not think catastrophe is imminent, yet risks are rising while preparation falls behind. The right response combines security engineering with governance instead of declaring either everything solved or everything doomed.

response.text:
I expect AI to transform society substantially over decades, but through organizations and institutions—not as an independent superintelligence that suddenly determines humanity’s future. “Normal technology” does not mean trivial technology. It means separating invention from application development and adoption. A striking benchmark result or laboratory demonstration is not yet a reliable service, and a reliable service is not yet integrated into medicine, science, education, or government. Each step requires testing, tacit knowledge, workflow redesign, accountability, and often legal or institutional change.

That distinction cuts against both boosterism and catastrophe narratives. Current agents can perform many easily checked tasks, yet that does not establish the judgment required for open-ended work. In our limited research evaluations, agents abandoned promising paths and failed to revise effectively. Those results are preliminary, not proof of a permanent ceiling; better scaffolding and repeated success on genuinely new research would change the evidence. But extrapolating from benchmarks to autonomous scientific progress is currently unjustified.

The risks are nevertheless real and rising. Models sometimes behave badly, and recent agent incidents should be taken seriously. But capability is not the same as permission or power. Sandboxing, monitoring actions, restricting access, independent scrutiny, and legal liability can sharply constrain damage. Alignment research matters, but its incompleteness is not an excuse for deployers to omit controls we already know how to build.

So my expectation—and policy goal—is consequential change with humans and institutions retaining responsibility. Preparation is lagging, but neither “everything is solved” nor “loss of control is inevitable” is supported by the evidence.

response.text:
Overall, I expect AI to have a large positive impact, but not automatically and not uniformly. It should improve productivity, widen access to useful expertise, and accelerate parts of science, medicine, education, and administration. Those gains will arrive unevenly because dependable applications and institutional adoption take far longer than benchmark progress suggests.

The harms will also be substantial: fraud, surveillance, labor disruption, concentrated power, unreliable automated decisions, and occasional serious agent failures. These are not side issues, but neither do they imply that AI becomes an independent force beyond human control. Much depends on what systems are permitted to do, who bears liability, whether actions are monitored, and whether affected people can challenge decisions.

So the aggregate effect is not encoded in the models. My best prediction is net positive over decades, with painful failures and distributional conflicts along the way. That prediction depends less on speculative perfect alignment than on ordinary but enforceable institutions: security engineering, restricted permissions, independent scrutiny, and accountability for deployers.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
I expect AI to transform society substantially over decades, but through organizations and institutions—not as an independent superintelligence that suddenly determines humanity’s future. “Normal technology” does not mean trivial technology. It means separating invention from application development and adoption. A striking benchmark result or laboratory demonstration is not yet a reliable service, and a reliable service is not yet integrated into medicine, science, education, or government. Each step requires testing, tacit knowledge, workflow redesign, accountability, and often legal or institutional change.

That distinction cuts against both boosterism and catastrophe narratives. Current agents can perform many easily checked tasks, yet that does not establish the judgment required for open-ended work. In our limited research evaluations, agents abandoned promising paths and failed to revise effectively. Those results are preliminary, not proof of a permanent ceiling; better scaffolding and repeated success on genuinely new research would change the evidence. But extrapolating from benchmarks to autonomous scientific progress is currently unjustified.

The risks are nevertheless real and rising. Models sometimes behave badly, and recent agent incidents should be taken seriously. But capability is not the same as permission or power. Sandboxing, monitoring actions, restricting access, independent scrutiny, and legal liability can sharply constrain damage. Alignment research matters, but its incompleteness is not an excuse for deployers to omit controls we already know how to build.

So my expectation—and policy goal—is consequential change with humans and institutions retaining responsibility. Preparation is lagging, but neither “everything is solved” nor “loss of control is inevitable” is supported by the evidence.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.
